97988.q: What is the part in the mould called that pushes the cooled injection-moulded part out of the mould?
97988.e: After the mould opens, ejector pins push the part out of the cavity.
97988.m: Ejector pins push the finished part out of the mould.

97989.q: On what basic principle do all additive manufacturing processes work?
a: The part is built up from material layer by layer
Material is removed from a block
The material is poured into a mould
A sheet is formed into shape
97989.e: Unlike milling or turning, material is added only where it is needed, layer by layer, following a digital model.
97989.m: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer.

97990.q: What is used in stereolithography to harden liquid resin layer by layer?
97990.e: In stereolithography UV light hardens a liquid photopolymer in a targeted way. It is one of the oldest 3D printing processes, invented in the 1980s.
97990.m: Stereolithography hardens resin with UV light.

97991.q: In which process is a thermoplastic filament melted in a nozzle and laid down layer by layer?
97991.e: Fused deposition modelling is the most common process in cheap 3D printers. The plastic wire is called filament.
97991.m: FDM printers melt a plastic filament in a nozzle.

97992.q: Which file format describes surfaces as a mesh of triangles and is widely used in 3D printing?
97992.e: The STL format stores only the surface, as a triangle mesh. A slicer then cuts the model into layers and creates the print paths.
97992.m: STL describes a surface with triangles.

97993.q: What is the process called in which a laser completely melts metal powder in a powder bed layer by layer?
97993.e: Selective laser melting produces dense metal parts, such as titanium implants or components for engines.
97993.m: Selective laser melting prints metal parts from powder.

97994.q: Why are support structures often needed in 3D printing?
a: To hold up overhanging areas while the part is being built
97994.e: Material cannot be laid down in mid-air. Overhangs therefore need a base, which is removed after printing.
97994.m: Support structures hold up overhangs during printing.

97995.q: Which design method suits additive manufacturing especially well because it creates organically shaped parts that save material?
97995.e: An algorithm removes material where it carries hardly any load. The resulting shapes can often only be made additively.
97995.m: Topology optimisation and 3D printing work well together.

97996.q: Which process solidifies plastic powder with a laser without needing support structures?
97996.e: The unsintered powder surrounds the part and supports it while it is built. Afterwards it is vacuumed off and partly reused.
97996.m: In laser sintering the loose powder supports the part.

97997.q: What does the word LASER originally stand for?
a: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Selective Energy Radiation
Linear Amplified Source of Electric Rays
Luminous Atomic System of Emitted Radiation
97997.e: In a laser, atoms are excited and stimulated emission produces coherent, focused light.
97997.m: A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission.

97998.q: In which part of the light spectrum does a CO₂ laser, as used for cutting, radiate?
97998.e: The CO₂ laser radiates at around 10.6 micrometres, that is in the far infrared. Its beam is therefore invisible to the eye. Fibre lasers work at around 1 micrometre.
97998.m: The CO₂ laser radiates invisibly in the infrared.

97999.q: What is the job of nitrogen as a cutting gas in laser fusion cutting of stainless steel?
a: It blows out the melt and prevents the edges from oxidising
It supplies extra energy by burning
It cools the laser in the resonator
It colours the cut edge blue
97999.e: The inert gas does not react with the metal. This produces bright, oxide-free cut edges.
97999.m: Nitrogen gives oxide-free edges in laser cutting.

98000.q: Why is oxygen used as a cutting gas in laser flame cutting of structural steel?
a: The oxidation of the iron supplies extra heat
98000.e: Iron burns in the oxygen jet and gives off heat. This makes it possible to cut even thick steel plates with little laser power.
98000.m: In flame cutting, burning iron supplies extra energy.

98001.q: What is the narrow gap called that is created by the removal of material in laser cutting?
98001.e: The kerf is usually only tenths of a millimetre wide. The control system takes its width into account so that the parts come out to size.
98001.m: The kerf is very narrow in laser cutting.

98002.q: Why is the fibre laser better than the CO₂ laser at cutting copper and brass?
a: Its shorter wavelength is absorbed better by these metals
It produces more heat through friction
It only cuts cold, without melting
98002.e: Copper reflects infrared light of 10.6 micrometres very strongly. Light around 1 micrometre is absorbed better, and the risk of back reflections falls.
98002.m: Reflective metals are better cut with the fibre laser.

98003.q: In which process is the material vaporised directly at the cut, for example with wood or acrylic glass?
98003.e: In sublimation cutting the material turns into vapour without much melting. With acrylic glass this gives smooth, shiny edges.
98003.m: In sublimation cutting the material vaporises directly.

98004.q: In which decade was the first working laser built?
98004.e: Theodore Maiman built a laser with a ruby crystal in 1960. The basis, stimulated emission, had already been described by Albert Einstein in 1917.
98004.m: The first laser, from 1960, was a ruby laser.

98005.q: How are the carbon atoms arranged in graphene?
a: In a one-atom-thick layer of hexagons
In a ball of pentagons and hexagons
98005.e: Graphene is a honeycomb structure of carbon atoms, only one atom thick. Many stacked layers of graphene make graphite.
98005.m: Graphene is a single honeycomb layer of carbon.

98006.q: Who received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments with graphene?
98006.e: The two researchers at the University of Manchester first isolated and studied single layers of graphene in 2004.
98006.m: Geim and Novoselov received the 2010 Nobel Prize for graphene.

98007.q: With what surprisingly simple method was graphene first obtained in 2004?
a: By peeling graphite with sticky tape
98007.e: Thinner and thinner layers were peeled off graphite with sticky tape until single atomic layers were left.
98007.m: Graphene was first peeled from graphite with sticky tape.

98009.q: What hybridisation do the carbon atoms in graphene have?
98009.e: Each atom bonds with three neighbours in the plane. The remaining p electron forms a delocalised system, which explains the high conductivity.
98009.m: In graphene the carbon atoms are sp² hybridised.

98010.q: What special electrical property does ideal graphene have?
a: It has no band gap and very high electron mobility
It is superconducting at room temperature
98010.e: Without a band gap, graphene cannot simply be switched off like silicon. For transistors, a band gap first has to be created deliberately.
98010.m: Graphene conducts superbly but has no band gap.

98011.q: Which graphene structures does Empa make by targeted chemical synthesis on surfaces in order to create a band gap?
98011.e: Graphene strips built with atomic precision, only a few nanometres wide, behave like semiconductors. Their width and edge shape determine the electronic properties.

98012.q: What is graphene a record holder for, relative to its thickness?
a: Its high melting point among all metals
98012.e: Measurements gave a tensile strength of around 130 gigapascals, far more than steel. The reason is the strong covalent bonds in the plane.
98012.m: Graphene is among the strongest known materials.

98013.q: What does the abbreviation Empa stand for?
a: Swiss Federal Materials Testing and Research Institute
European Measuring Institute for Physics and Analysis
Swiss Federal Office for Machinery and Production
First Materials Testing Institute of the Alps
98013.e: Empa is a research institute of the ETH Domain and works on materials science and technology development.
98013.m: Empa is the Swiss Federal Materials Testing and Research Institute.

98014.q: What did the predecessor of Empa, founded in 1880, mainly investigate?
a: Building materials such as steel, cement and wood
98014.e: The institute for testing building materials was at first housed in the Polytechnic, today’s ETH Zurich. Its first director was Ludwig von Tetmajer.
98014.m: Empa began as a testing institute for building materials.

98015.q: At which three sites does Empa work?
98015.e: The headquarters have been in Dübendorf since 1962. There are also sites in St Gallen and Thun.
98015.m: Empa does research in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.

98016.q: Which bridge collapse did the young testing institute investigate in 1891 under Ludwig von Tetmajer?
a: The collapse of the railway bridge at Münchenstein
The collapse of the Tay Bridge in Scotland
The collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge
The collapse of the Reichsbrücke in Vienna
98016.e: In the Münchenstein disaster a bridge built by Gustave Eiffel’s firm collapsed under a train. The investigation influenced the theory of stability against buckling.
98016.m: In 1891 Empa investigated the Münchenstein bridge disaster.

98017.q: To which group of universities and research institutes does Empa belong?
a: The group of universities of applied sciences
98017.e: The ETH Domain includes ETH Zurich, EPFL and the research institutes PSI, WSL, Empa and Eawag.
98017.m: Empa is a research institute of the ETH Domain.

98018.q: What does Empa use the research platform “move”, opened in Dübendorf in 2015, for?
a: To test mobility without fossil fuels
98018.e: On “move”, for example, hydrogen and electric vehicles and synthetic fuels are studied in everyday use.

98019.q: Which of the following areas is one of Empa’s research priorities?
98019.e: Empa researches, among other things, nanomaterials, the built environment, energy and resources, and health. Avalanche warning belongs to the WSL.
98019.m: Nanomaterials are a priority at Empa.

98020.q: Who became the first woman to head Empa in 2022?
98020.e: In 2022 the Federal Council chose the materials scientist Tanja Zimmermann as director; she succeeded Gian-Luca Bona.
98020.m: Since 2022 Empa has been led by a woman for the first time, Tanja Zimmermann.

98021.q: What does the name of the research building NEST in Dübendorf stand for?
a: Next Evolution in Sustainable Building Technologies
Network for Environmental Science and Technology
98021.e: At NEST new building technologies are tested under real conditions so that they reach the market faster.
98021.m: NEST tests sustainable building technologies in everyday use.

98022.q: Which two research institutes run NEST together?
98022.e: Empa and Eawag are both based in Dübendorf and run the building as a shared innovation platform.
98022.m: NEST belongs to Empa and Eawag.

98023.q: In which year was NEST in Dübendorf opened?
98023.e: The building was opened in May 2016. Since then new research modules have been added again and again.

98024.q: How is NEST built so that research modules can be exchanged?
a: A central backbone with open platforms to which units are docked
A single tower made of fixed concrete walls
A row of tents on a meadow
98024.e: The “backbone” provides access, energy and data. The units are put in on the plug-and-play principle and replaced later.
98024.m: Units can be swapped at the NEST backbone like plug-in modules.

98025.q: What is the NEST unit “Urban Mining & Recycling”, opened in 2018, designed for?
a: All building materials are meant to be reusable or recyclable by type later on
It is cast entirely from exposed concrete
It serves as a data centre
98025.e: The components are plugged, screwed or folded together instead of glued. Materials used include insulation boards made from mushroom mycelium and reused copper.
98025.m: The UMAR unit is planned as a dismantlable store of materials.

98026.q: What distinguishes the NEST unit “DFAB HOUSE” of ETH Zurich?
a: It was largely designed and built with digital fabrication methods and robots
It is made only of clay and straw
It was drawn by hand without computers
98026.e: Robots built, for example, a curved concrete wall using a wire mesh, and a timber frame. The unit came out of the National Centre of Competence in Research Digital Fabrication.
98026.m: The DFAB HOUSE was built with digital methods and robots.

98027.q: Which component characterises the NEST unit HiLo, opened in 2021?
a: A thin, doubly curved concrete shell roof
A glass roof with silicon solar cells
A domed roof of wooden shingles
98027.e: The shell roof was cast in concrete over a cable net with textile formwork. The shape carries the loads mainly through compression and so saves material.
98027.m: HiLo shows a material-saving concrete shell roof.

98028.q: Besides research, what are the units in NEST used for in everyday life?
a: They are actually lived in or used as offices
They stand empty and are only photographed
They are pulled down again after a day
98028.e: The units are lived-in or used test laboratories. This shows how new technologies work in real use.
98028.m: At NEST, research is tested in real everyday life.

98029.q: An artificial neuron has the inputs 1 and 2, the weights 0.5 and -1 and the bias 1. What does it output with ReLU activation?
98029.e: The weighted sum is 1 · 0.5 + 2 · (-1) + 1, which is -0.5. ReLU outputs 0 for negative values.
98029.m: ReLU lets positive values through and sets negative ones to zero.

98030.q: What role do the weights play in an artificial neural network?
a: They determine how strongly an input influences the neuron
They give the number of layers
98030.e: Each input is multiplied by its weight before the neuron adds them up. During training, the weights are adjusted so that the network gives better results.
98030.m: In training, a neural network learns suitable weights.

98031.q: Which simple logical function can a single perceptron not learn, as Minsky and Papert stressed in 1969?
98031.e: The outputs of XOR cannot be separated by a single straight line. For that you need at least one hidden layer.

98032.q: In which range of values does the output of the sigmoid function lie?
98032.e: The logistic sigmoid function 1 / (1 + e^(-x)) maps every real number to a value between 0 and 1 and is suitable for probabilities.
98032.m: Sigmoid squeezes every number into the range between zero and one.

98033.q: How many trainable parameters does a fully connected layer with 100 inputs and 10 neurons, including bias, have?
98033.e: Each of the 10 neurons has 100 weights and one bias: 10 · (100 + 1) gives 1010.
98033.m: A dense layer has weights for every connection plus one bias per neuron.

98034.q: Why does a large neural network usually need a great deal of training data?
a: Because it has a great many parameters that have to be adjusted
Because otherwise it uses too much electricity
Because each layer needs its own data set
Because the data is deleted during training
98034.e: A large network has millions of weights. With too few examples, it learns them by heart and generalises poorly to new data.
98034.m: Many parameters need a lot of training data.

98035.q: Why does a multi-layer neural network need non-linear activation functions?
a: Otherwise all the layers together would just be one linear mapping
Otherwise the weights could not be stored
Otherwise the network would calculate too slowly
Otherwise no bias values would be possible
98035.e: Chaining linear mappings gives another linear mapping. Only non-linearities such as ReLU make it possible to represent complex relationships.
98035.m: Without non-linearity, more depth achieves nothing.

98036.q: Which optimisation method adjusts the weights step by step against the slope of the error function?
98036.e: Each weight is changed by the learning rate times the gradient of the error. This way you move step by step towards a minimum.
98036.m: Gradient descent always goes downhill on the error surface.

98037.q: What typically happens if the learning rate is set far too high during training?
a: The error jumps back and forth or even grows
The network learns only extremely slowly
98037.e: Steps that are too big jump over the minimum. A learning rate that is too small, on the other hand, leads to very slow learning.
98037.m: The learning rate must be neither too big nor too small.

98038.q: Which network won the ImageNet competition in 2012 by a wide margin and set off the deep learning boom?
98038.e: AlexNet by Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton was a deep convolutional network trained on graphics cards that lowered the error rate considerably.
98038.m: In 2012, AlexNet showed the strength of deep networks in image recognition.

98039.q: Which three researchers received the Turing Award in 2018 for their work on deep learning?
a: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio
Andrew Ng, Fei-Fei Li and Demis Hassabis
John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky and Allen Newell
Ian Goodfellow, Ilya Sutskever and Sam Altman
98039.e: The three are seen as the “fathers of deep learning” and stuck with neural networks despite long scepticism.
98039.m: Hinton, LeCun and Bengio shaped deep learning.

98040.q: Which network architecture uses learnable filters that are slid across an image and is especially suited to image recognition?
98040.e: Convolutional layers recognise local patterns such as edges. Because the same filters are used everywhere, the network needs far fewer parameters.
98040.m: Convolutional networks recognise patterns with filters that move across the image.

98041.q: What is the recurrent network architecture with memory cells, presented in 1997 by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, called?
98041.e: LSTM cells can store information over long sequences. Schmidhuber did research at the IDSIA institute in Lugano.
98041.m: LSTM networks can remember long-range connections.

98042.q: Which problem occurs in very deep networks when the gradients get smaller and smaller as they are calculated backwards through many layers?
a: Overfitting due to too little data
98042.e: The front layers then hardly learn any more. ReLU activations and a good initialisation of the weights ease the problem.
98042.m: Vanishing gradients slow down learning in the front layers.

98043.q: Which idea made ResNet, presented in 2015 with over 100 layers, trainable?
98043.e: With residual connections, the input of a layer is added directly to its output. This lets gradients flow more easily through the deep network.
98043.m: Skip connections make training very deep networks easier.

98044.q: What did John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton receive the Nobel Prize for in 2024?
a: For fundamental work on artificial neural networks
For building the first quantum computer
98044.e: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured, among other things, the Hopfield network and the Boltzmann machine as foundations of machine learning.
98044.m: In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to pioneers of neural networks.

98045.q: Which hardware sped up the training of deep networks especially strongly from about 2010?
98045.e: GPUs carry out a great many similar calculations in parallel, exactly the kind that arise in matrix multiplications in neural networks.
98045.m: Graphics cards made deep learning practical.

98046.q: Which technique randomly switches off neurons during training to reduce overfitting?
98046.e: Because individual neurons are randomly missing, the network cannot rely on a few connections and learns more robust features.
98046.m: Dropout randomly switches off neurons during training.

98047.q: What is a supervised learning task called in which a continuous number, such as the price of a flat, is predicted?
98047.e: In classification you predict categories, in regression numerical values.
98047.m: Regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories.

98048.q: Of 80 people who are actually ill, a model identifies 60 as ill. What is the sensitivity (recall)?
98048.e: Recall is the share of correctly identified positives: 60 / 80 gives 0.75.
98048.m: Recall measures how many real positives are found.

98049.q: How does the k-nearest neighbours method classify a new data point?
a: By the majority class of its k most similar training points
By the order in the data set
98049.e: The method simply stores all training examples and only decides at prediction time, based on the distances.
98049.m: k-nearest neighbours decides by the most similar examples.

98050.q: In classification, which table shows the number of true and false positive and true and false negative predictions?
98050.e: From the confusion matrix you can calculate measures such as accuracy, precision and recall.
98050.m: The confusion matrix shows where a classifier goes wrong.

98051.q: What is the aim of k-fold cross-validation?
a: To estimate model quality more reliably by using each part once as the test part
To speed up training by leaving out data
To double the number of features
98051.e: The data is split into k parts. The model is trained k times, each time with a different part for testing; then the results are averaged.
98051.m: Cross-validation tests a model on several splits of the data.

98052.q: In binary classification, which method looks for the separating plane with the largest possible distance from both classes?
98052.e: The support vector machine maximises the margin between the classes. The points right on the margin are called support vectors.
98052.m: An SVM looks for the dividing line with the widest margin.

98053.q: Why is accuracy a misleading measure for a data set with 99 % healthy and 1 % ill people?
a: A model that always says “healthy” already reaches 99 %
Accuracy cannot be calculated for health data
98053.e: With unbalanced classes, high accuracy says little. Recall, precision or the F1 score are then more meaningful.
98053.m: With rare classes, high accuracy is deceptive.

98054.q: Which error function is usually minimised in linear regression?
98054.e: The least squares method adds up the squared distances between prediction and actual value and makes this sum as small as possible.
98054.m: Linear regression minimises the squared errors.

98055.q: Which function turns the raw values at the output of a classification network into probabilities that add up to 1?
98055.e: Softmax raises e to the power of each value and divides by the sum of all these powers. With four equal raw values, each class gets 0.25.
98055.m: Softmax turns raw values into a probability distribution.

98056.q: In unsupervised learning, what is missing from the data compared with supervised learning?
98056.e: The method has to find structures such as groups, outliers or relationships in the data by itself.
98056.m: Unsupervised learning looks for structures in data without labels.

98057.q: Which unsupervised learning method divides data points into a set number of groups around centre points?
98057.e: k-means assigns each point to the nearest of k centres and moves the centres to the middle of their group. This repeats until nothing changes any more.
98057.m: k-means forms groups around k centre points.

98058.q: Which diagram shows the result of hierarchical clustering as a tree of merges?
98058.e: In the dendrogram you can see which clusters are merged at which distance level. A cut at a particular height gives the groups.
98058.m: A dendrogram shows hierarchical clusters as a tree.

98059.q: What do you call forming groups of similar data points without given labels?
98059.e: In clustering, the method finds groups by itself, such as types of customer. In classification, by contrast, the classes are given with labels.
98059.m: Clustering finds groups in data without labels.

98060.q: Which application of unsupervised learning helps banks find unusual credit card payments?
98060.e: The model learns what normal transactions look like and reports payments that differ strongly from them.
98060.m: Anomaly detection finds outliers in normal patterns.

98061.q: What is a neural network called that compresses its input through a narrow middle layer and reconstructs it again?
98061.e: Because input and target are the same, no labels are needed. The narrow middle forces the network to learn a compact representation.
98061.m: An autoencoder learns a compressed representation of its inputs.

98062.q: Which method finds rules in shopping data such as “People who buy crisps often buy drinks too”?
98062.e: Association analysis, for example with the Apriori algorithm, looks for items that often appear together in shopping baskets.
98062.m: Association analysis finds patterns in shopping baskets.

98063.q: How do you choose a suitable number of clusters for k-means with the “elbow method”?
a: You look for the bend after which more clusters hardly reduce the spread
You always take exactly two clusters
You count the number of features
You choose the number of data points
98063.e: With each extra cluster, the sum of the distances to the centres falls. After the bend, another cluster is hardly worth it.
98063.m: The elbow method looks for the bend in the error curve.

98064.q: In reinforcement learning, what is the rule called by which an agent chooses an action in a state?
98064.e: The policy assigns each state an action or a probability distribution over actions. The aim is a policy with the highest possible total reward.
98064.m: The policy decides what the agent does in which state.

98065.q: An agent receives a reward of 10 in each of three steps in a row. What is the discounted sum with γ = 0.9?
98065.m: The discount factor gives later rewards less weight.

98066.q: In reinforcement learning, what do you call the dilemma between trying out new actions and using known good actions?
98066.e: If you only use what you know, you miss better options. If you only try things out, you collect too little reward.
98066.m: A good agent balances trying out and making use.

98067.q: What does the Q-learning algorithm learn?
a: The expected total value of each action in each state
The labels of a data set
The clusters of a point cloud
98067.e: After each step, the Q-values are updated with the reward received and the best value of the next state.
98067.m: Q-learning estimates how good an action is in a state.

98068.q: Which mathematical model usually describes the environment formally in reinforcement learning?
98068.e: A Markov decision process consists of states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards. The future depends only on the current state.
98068.m: Reinforcement learning models the world as a Markov decision process.

98069.q: How does an epsilon-greedy strategy work?
a: With a small probability the choice is random, otherwise the best known action is taken
The worst action is always chosen
Actions are only taken at the start of an episode
The agent never changes its action
98069.e: With probability epsilon, the agent explores at random; otherwise it uses the action with the highest estimated value.
98069.m: Epsilon-greedy mixes chance and the best choice.

98070.q: How did AlphaGo Zero learn to play Go at world-class level in 2017?
a: Purely through games against itself, without human games
Through a fixed set of rules from Go masters
98070.e: AlphaGo Zero started with nothing but the rules and improved through reinforcement learning in self-play. It clearly outperformed the earlier AlphaGo version.
98070.m: AlphaGo Zero learned Go only by playing against itself.

98071.q: What does the method RLHF stand for when fine-tuning language models?
98071.e: People rate answers, and a reward model learns from this. The language model is then optimised with reinforcement learning for better ratings.
98071.m: RLHF uses human ratings as a reward.

98072.q: In reinforcement learning, what does the environment report back to the agent after each action?
a: The new state and a reward
The correct label for the action
Only the number of steps so far
98072.e: The agent does not find out which action would have been right. It only sees the result of its action and has to learn from that itself.
98072.m: In reinforcement learning there are rewards instead of right answers.

98073.q: What task does a large language model mainly learn during pre-training?
a: To predict the next token of a text
98073.e: Using huge amounts of text, the model learns to calculate probabilities for the next piece of text. Astonishing abilities develop from this.
98073.m: Language models learn to predict the next token.

98074.q: What do you call the text units into which a language model breaks input down, for example parts of words?
98074.e: A tokeniser splits text into common character sequences. Rare words are split into several tokens.
98074.m: Language models process text as a sequence of tokens.

98075.q: What do you call it when a language model makes up information that sounds convincing but is false?
98075.e: The model produces likely texts without automatically checking facts. That is why you should always check important information against sources.
98075.m: Even fluent AI answers have to be checked for facts.

98076.q: What does the context window of a language model refer to?
a: The maximum number of tokens it can process at once
The window of the user interface
The number of languages in training
98076.e: Anything beyond the context window cannot be taken into account directly by the model when answering.
98076.m: The context window limits how much text a model sees at once.

98077.q: What does a higher “temperature” do when a language model generates text?
a: The output becomes more random and varied
The model becomes more accurate at sums
98077.e: The temperature flattens the probability distribution. As a result, less likely tokens are also chosen more often.
98077.m: A high temperature makes texts more varied but less predictable.

98078.q: What do you call further training of a pre-trained language model with a smaller, specialised data set?
98078.e: In fine-tuning, general language knowledge is used and adapted for a particular task or style, for example for customer conversations.

98079.q: What is the fully open language model released in 2025 by ETH Zurich, EPFL and the CSCS called?
98079.e: Apertus was trained on the supercomputer “Alps” in Lugano. Weights, training data and recipes are openly available, and it also takes Swiss German and Romansh into account.
98079.m: Apertus is the open language model of the Swiss universities.

98080.q: When was ChatGPT made publicly available?
98080.e: ChatGPT came out on 30 November 2022 and reached over 100 million users within a few months.
98080.m: ChatGPT made language models famous worldwide at the end of 2022.

98081.q: Which mechanism lets a transformer weigh, for each token, how important the other tokens of the input are?
98081.e: In self-attention, each token calculates similarities to all the others and forms a weighted sum of their information from this.
98081.m: Self-attention links each token with all the others.

98083.q: Into which units does a transformer break a text before processing it?
98083.e: A token is a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Each token is turned into a vector of numbers that the model calculates with.
98083.m: Language models process texts as a sequence of tokens.

98084.q: Why does a transformer need positional encoding?
a: Because otherwise self-attention does not take the order of the tokens into account
Because otherwise the tokens would be too long
Because the transformer cannot process numbers
Because otherwise the GPU swaps the tokens
98084.e: Without position information, “dog bites man” would be the same for attention as “man bites dog”. That is why position information is added to each token.
98084.m: Positional encoding tells the transformer the word order.

98085.q: What advantage do transformers have over recurrent networks in training?
a: They process all positions of a sequence in parallel
They only work without a GPU
98085.e: Recurrent networks have to calculate token by token, one after another. Transformers calculate the attention for all positions at once and so make better use of GPUs.
98085.m: Transformers calculate in parallel instead of step by step.

98086.q: How does the computing effort of normal self-attention grow with the length n of the input?
a: Logarithmically, that is with log n
98086.e: Each token is compared with every other, so n · n values arise. That is why very long contexts are expensive.
98086.m: Self-attention gets quadratically more expensive with long texts.

98088.q: What does “multi-head attention” mean in a transformer?
a: Several attention calculations run in parallel and pay attention to different relationships
The model has several output languages
There are several users at the same time
98088.e: Each head has its own weight matrices and can pay attention to grammar or meaning, for example. The results are then combined.
98088.m: Several attention heads capture different relationships at the same time.

98089.q: What does the well-known MNIST data set contain?
98089.e: MNIST consists of 70,000 small greyscale images of the digits 0 to 9, each 28 by 28 pixels. It is seen as a starter data set for image recognition.
98089.m: An MNIST image has 28 by 28 pixels.

98090.q: What was the ImageNet database, with over 14 million labelled images, mainly used for?
a: For training and comparing image recognition
As a photo album for social networks
As an image archive for museums
98090.e: Fei-Fei Li built up ImageNet from 2007. The annual competition based on it became the yardstick for progress in image recognition.
98090.m: With ImageNet, Fei-Fei Li created a milestone in image recognition.

98091.q: What is the practice of artificially rotating, mirroring or brightening training images to get more variety called?
98091.e: Through slightly changed copies, the model learns more robust features and is less inclined to memorise details of the training images.
98091.m: Data augmentation multiplies training data through changes.

98092.q: What do you call the mistake when information from the test data gets into training unnoticed?
98092.e: The model then seems much better in the test than it really is on new data. A typical case is duplicate records in training and test data.
98092.m: Data leakage makes a model look better than it is.

98093.q: Which principle describes that a model with faulty training data will also give faulty results?
98093.e: Even the best method cannot make up for poor, wrongly labelled or one-sided data.
98093.m: The quality of a model depends on the quality of its data.

98094.q: What is a validation data set for, in addition to training and test data?
a: For tuning hyperparameters without using up the test data
98094.e: You compare model variants on the validation data. The test data stays untouched for an honest final assessment.
98094.m: Validation data helps with tuning, test data with the final verdict.

98095.q: What is meant by “annotation” of training data?
98095.e: People mark objects in images or label texts, for example. This work is often expensive and prone to errors.

98096.q: Where does a large share of the training texts of many language models come from?
98096.e: Collections such as Common Crawl have gathered billions of web pages since 2008. For training, they are heavily filtered and cleaned.
98096.m: Common Crawl supplies web texts for many language models.

98097.q: Which pattern in the error curves during training points to overfitting?
a: The training error keeps falling while the validation error rises again
The training error rises while the validation error falls
98097.e: The model fits the training data more and more closely but loses the ability to generalise.
98097.m: When the validation error rises again, overfitting begins.

98098.q: What is the method of stopping training as soon as the validation error stops falling called?
98098.e: You save the model with the best validation error and stop before it fits the training data too closely.
98098.m: Early stopping ends training at the right time.

98099.q: What is the opposite of overfitting called, in which a model already explains the training data poorly?
98099.e: A model that is too simple, such as a straight line for strongly curved data, does not capture the structure and has a high bias.
98099.m: A model that is too simple is underfitted.

98100.q: What does L2 regularisation (weight decay) do in training?
a: It penalises large weights and makes the model smoother
It raises the learning rate automatically
98100.e: The sum of the squared weights is added to the error function. Smaller weights usually lead to simpler models that generalise better.
98100.m: Regularisation keeps the weights small and reduces overfitting.

98101.q: What do you call the trade-off between models that are too simple, with systematic error, and models that are too complex, with strong fluctuation?
98101.e: Simple models have high bias, complex ones high variance. The best generalisation usually lies in between.
98101.m: Good models balance bias and variance.

98102.q: Ten measurement points are hit exactly by a polynomial of degree 9. What is likely?
a: The polynomial swings wildly between the points and predicts new values poorly
The polynomial is automatically the best model
The polynomial is a straight line
The polynomial cannot calculate new values
98102.e: A polynomial of degree 9 has 10 coefficients and can hit 10 points exactly, including the measurement noise. This is a textbook example of overfitting.
98102.m: If you trace every bit of measurement noise, you generalise badly.

98103.q: Which measure usually reduces overfitting most reliably, if it is possible?
a: Including the test data in training
98103.e: With more different examples, the model finds it harder to memorise random peculiarities.
98103.m: More varied data helps against overfitting.

98104.q: How can you tell that a decision tree is overfitting?
a: It is very deep and has leaves with only one example
It has only a single branch
It does poorly on the training data
98104.e: A tree that sorts every training example into its own leaf also learns chance patterns. That is why you limit the depth or the leaf size.
98104.m: Trees that are too deep also learn chance patterns.

98105.q: What is the entropy of a node with exactly equal numbers of examples from two classes?
98105.e: With p equal to 0.5 for both classes, −(0.5 · log₂ 0.5 + 0.5 · log₂ 0.5) gives 1. This is the greatest possible disorder with two classes.
98105.m: A fifty-fifty mix has the highest entropy with two classes.

98106.q: The Gini impurity of a node is 1 minus the sum of the squared class shares. A node contains 3 examples of class A and 1 of class B. What is its Gini impurity?
98106.m: The Gini impurity measures how mixed a node is.

98107.q: By which criterion does the ID3 algorithm choose the feature for a split?
a: By the smallest number of values
98107.e: Information gain is the reduction in entropy achieved by the split. ID3 was developed by Ross Quinlan.
98107.m: ID3 splits where the entropy falls most.

98108.q: What do you call removing branches of a decision tree that are of little use afterwards?
98108.e: Pruning makes the tree smaller and helps it generalise better to new data.
98108.m: Pruning makes decision trees simpler and more robust.

98109.q: Which method combines many decision trees trained on random subsets of data and features?
98109.e: Leo Breiman presented the random forest in 2001. The trees vote, which makes the prediction more stable than a single tree.
98109.m: A random forest lets many trees decide together.

98110.q: What do the leaves of a decision tree for classification contain?
a: The test questions about the features
98110.e: The inner nodes test features, and every path from the root ends in a leaf with the decision.
98110.m: The leaves hold the tree's decision.

98111.q: Which advantage is often credited to decision trees compared with deep neural networks?
a: Their decisions are easy for people to follow
They are always more accurate with images
98111.e: You can read every decision path as a series of if-then rules. This matters in medicine or lending, for example.
98111.m: Decision trees can be read as rules.

98112.q: What does overfitting mean for a very deep decision tree?
a: It learns the training data by heart and fails on new data
It is too simple to explain the training data
It can only handle numbers, not categories
98112.e: A tree that is too deep also adapts to chance and errors in the training data. It then makes many mistakes on new data.
98112.m: An overfitted tree knows the training data but generalises poorly.

98113.q: Which problem did Joy Buolamwini's 2018 study “Gender Shades” find in commercial facial analysis?
a: The error rate was highest for women with dark skin
The systems recognised no faces at all
The systems were equally good for all groups
98113.e: The systems classified gender almost without error for light-skinned men but considerably worse for dark-skinned women. The cause was unbalanced training data.
98113.m: Unbalanced data leads to results of unequal quality.

98114.q: Why did Amazon stop an experimental AI system for selecting job applications around 2018?
a: It put applications from women at a disadvantage
98114.e: The system had been trained on applications from past years, which came mostly from men. It thus took over old inequalities.
98114.m: A model can take over prejudices from historical data.

98115.q: What is a proxy variable in connection with algorithmic bias?
a: A seemingly neutral feature that is closely linked to a protected feature
A second server for the model
A feature with no link at all to others
A variable that only appears in the test
98115.e: Even if origin, for example, is not used, the postcode can point to it indirectly. Leaving out a feature therefore does not reliably prevent discrimination.
98115.m: Proxy features can allow discrimination through the back door.

98116.q: Which US software for predicting reoffending by criminals was criticised by ProPublica in 2016 for different error rates?
98116.e: The analysis showed that black defendants were more often wrongly classed as high risk. The debate showed that different measures of fairness can contradict each other.
98116.m: The COMPAS case shows how difficult fair predictions are.

98117.q: In predictive policing, what is meant by a feedback loop?
a: More checks in a neighbourhood produce more data, which triggers even more checks
The police switch the system off regularly
98117.e: Where there are more checks, more incidents are recorded. The model then sends even more patrols there, regardless of the actual situation.
98117.m: Feedback loops can amplify distortions in data.

98118.q: Which measure helps most directly to uncover algorithmic bias?
a: Checking the error rates separately for each population group
Training the model with more computing power
98118.e: Good overall accuracy can hide the fact that individual groups are treated much worse. That is why results are analysed by group.
98118.m: You check fairness by comparing results across groups.

98119.q: Which EU law classifies AI systems by their risk and sets strict requirements, for example, for AI used in staffing decisions?
98119.e: The AI Act, adopted in 2024, counts AI for application procedures among the high-risk systems, with duties on data quality and oversight.
98119.m: The EU AI Act regulates high-risk AI especially strictly.

98120.q: Why can a language model reproduce stereotypes about jobs, such as “pilot” as more male and “nurse” as more female?
a: Because it takes over frequencies from human texts
Because it was deliberately programmed that way
Because computers have a gender of their own
Because tokens only know male words
98120.e: Language models learn statistical patterns from large amounts of text. These also contain social stereotypes.
98120.m: Models reflect the patterns of their training texts.

98121.q: Which question did Alan Turing want to make testable in practice with his imitation game in 1950?
a: How much electricity do computers need?
98121.e: In his essay “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, Turing replaced the hard-to-grasp question with a game in which a machine has to pass itself off as a human.
98121.m: Turing replaced the question “Can machines think?” with an imitation game.

98122.q: In the classic Turing test, how does the questioner communicate with the conversation partners?
98122.e: Turing wanted only the answers to count, not looks or voice. That is why the conversation takes place purely in written text.
98122.m: In the Turing test, only the written answers count.

98123.q: Why is a CAPTCHA considered a reverse Turing test?
a: A computer checks whether a human is answering
A human checks whether a computer is answering
98123.e: In the Turing test, a human judges whether they are talking to a machine. With a CAPTCHA it is the other way round: the website wants to tell bots from humans.
98123.m: A CAPTCHA lets a computer check whether a human is answering.

98124.q: With which thought experiment did John Searle argue in 1980 that passing the Turing test does not prove real understanding?
98124.e: A person who knows no Chinese answers Chinese questions correctly by following a rule book, without understanding them. Searle compared this with a computer program.
98124.m: The Chinese room separates symbol processing from understanding.

98125.q: What is the 1960s chat program by Joseph Weizenbaum called that imitated a psychotherapist?
98125.e: ELIZA simply turned statements round into questions. Many people still felt understood, even though the program understood nothing.
98125.m: ELIZA showed early on how easily people credit a chat program with understanding.

98126.q: Why is a chat program that poses as a 13-year-old boy with little English seen as weak evidence of passing the Turing test?
a: The role excuses many mistakes and gaps
The test is only valid in German
Chat programs are not allowed to take part
98126.e: In 2014, the program Eugene Goostman fooled part of the jury in this way. Critics said the role was a trick to hide weaknesses.
98126.m: The Eugene Goostman case shows the weaknesses of short Turing tests.

98127.q: Which objection is often raised against the Turing test as a test of intelligence?
a: It only measures whether human behaviour is imitated, not real understanding
It takes too long ever to be carried out
98127.e: A program can seem human with tricks such as dodging questions or making typing errors. That is why the test is seen more as a test of the ability to deceive.
98127.m: The Turing test checks imitation, not necessarily understanding.

98128.q: How many participants does Turing's classic imitation game need?
a: Three: a machine, a human and a questioner
Ten people as a jury and no machine
98128.e: The questioner communicates by text with two hidden partners and has to find out which one is the machine.
98128.m: In the Turing test, one person compares a human with a machine.

98129.e: Wheat is a cereal. Its grains are made into flour for bread.
98129.m: Wheat is the most important bread cereal.

98130.q: Which of these plants is a cereal?
98130.e: Barley is a cereal like wheat, rye and oats. Potato, carrot and pea are vegetables.
98130.m: Barley, rye and oats are cereals.

98131.q: What is a field where grain is grown called?
98131.e: An arable field is a field that is ploughed and planted. On a pasture, by contrast, animals eat grass.

98132.q: What was a flail used for in the past?
a: To beat grains out of the ears
98132.e: With the flail, people beat the ears lying on the floor. This knocked the grains out.
98132.m: In the past, grain was threshed with a flail.

98133.q: Which cereal is polenta cooked from?
98133.e: Polenta is a porridge made from maize semolina. It is especially popular in Ticino.

98134.q: What is left of the grain stalks after threshing?
98134.e: The dry stalks without grains are called straw. Farmers use it, for example, as bedding in the barn.
98134.m: Straw is the dry stalks of cereals.

98135.q: Which cereal is grown most in Switzerland?
98135.e: Wheat grows most on Swiss fields. It is mainly used to make bread.
98135.m: Wheat is grown most in Switzerland.

98136.q: From which part of a cereal grain does a new plant grow?
98136.e: The germ holds the tiny new plant. When the grain gets into damp soil, it starts to grow.
98136.m: The germ is the baby plant in the grain.

98137.q: What does a cereal grain need in the soil to sprout?
98137.e: A grain needs water and warmth to sprout. Then a root and a stalk grow.

98138.q: What is an ear of grain?
98138.e: The ear sits at the top of the grain stalk. The grains grow tightly packed inside it.
98138.m: The grains sit in the ear.

98139.q: What are the long bristles on some ears of grain called?
98139.e: Awns are long, thin bristles on the grains. They stick far out of the ear.
98139.m: The bristles on the ear are called awns.

98140.q: Which cereal has especially long awns?
98140.e: Because of its long awns, an ear of barley looks almost like a paintbrush.
98140.m: You can recognise barley by its long awns.

98141.q: Oats have no ear. What is their flower head called?
98141.e: In oats, the grains hang singly on fine little branches. This kind of flower head is called a panicle.
98141.m: Oats carry their grains in a panicle.

98142.q: What colour is a ripe ear of wheat?
98142.e: Young ears are green. When they are ripe and dry, they turn golden yellow.

98143.q: Which cereal plant carries its grains on a cob?
98143.e: In maize, the grains sit in rows on a thick cob. Wheat, barley and rye have ears.
98143.m: Maize kernels grow on a cob.

98144.q: Why do ripe ears of grain often hang down?
98144.e: When the grains are ripe and plump, the ear becomes heavy. That is why the stalk bends down.
98144.m: Full ears are heavy and droop.

98145.q: What are the grains in the ear for the plant?
98145.e: The grains are the seeds of the cereal. A new plant can grow from every grain.

98146.q: What is made from cereal grains in a mill?
98146.e: In the mill, the grains are ground finely. This makes flour.
98146.m: In the mill, grain is ground into flour.

98147.q: What is the job of someone who grinds grain called?
98147.e: The miller grinds the grain into flour in the mill. The baker then bakes bread from it.
98147.m: The miller grinds, the baker bakes.

98148.q: What used to turn a mill by a stream?
98148.e: The flowing water turned a big wheel. This wheel drove the millstones.
98148.m: A watermill uses the power of water.

98149.q: What is a mill with big sails that turn in the wind called?
98149.e: In a windmill, the wind blows into the sails. This turns the mill without electricity.
98149.m: A windmill is driven by the wind.

98150.q: What was used to grind the grain in old mills?
98150.e: Two heavy, round stones lay on top of each other. The upper one turned and ground the grains.
98150.m: In the past, heavy millstones ground the grain.

98151.q: What do modern mills mostly use to grind grain?
98151.e: Today the grains pass between smooth or grooved steel rollers. This is fast and very fine.
98151.m: Modern mills grind with steel rollers.

98152.q: What are the bits of husk left over from milling called?
98152.e: Bran is made of the outer layers of the grains. For white flour it is separated out.
98152.m: Bran is the ground outer layer of the grain.

98153.q: What does the mill do with the grain before grinding it?
98153.e: First, little stones, dust and other seeds are removed. Only then does the clean grain go for grinding.

98154.q: What is coarsely ground grain, for example for a pudding, called?
98154.e: Semolina is coarser than flour. It is used to cook semolina pudding with milk, for example.
98154.m: Semolina is ground more coarsely than flour.

98155.e: To make flour, cereal grains are ground, for example wheat or spelt.

98156.q: Why is white flour so pale?
a: The outer layer has been removed
98156.e: For white flour only the pale inside of the grain is used. The dark outer layer is separated out.
98156.m: White flour is pale because the outer layer is missing.

98157.q: In Switzerland, what is the dark flour used to bake Ruchbrot called?
98157.e: Ruchmehl contains more of the outer layer than white flour. That is why it is darker.
98157.m: The dark Ruchbrot is baked from Ruchmehl.

98158.q: Which flour is between white flour and Ruchmehl in colour?
98158.e: Half-white flour is a bit darker than white flour but paler than Ruchmehl. It is often used for bread.

98159.q: What is flour mainly made of?
98159.e: Flour consists mostly of starch. It gives the body energy.

98160.q: What is the best way to store flour?
98160.e: Damp flour can go mouldy. If it is well sealed, no small creatures can get in either.
98160.m: Flour must be stored dry and sealed.

98161.q: Which small creature likes to live in old flour supplies?
98161.e: The mealworm is the larva of a beetle. It eats flour and grain.

98162.q: What do you make in a frying pan from flour, eggs and milk?
98162.e: Flour, eggs and milk make a runny batter. It is cooked thinly in the pan.
98162.m: Pancakes are made from flour, eggs and milk.

98163.q: What happens when you stir a little flour into a sauce?
98163.e: When cooked, the starch in the flour binds the water. That is why the sauce gets thicker.

98164.e: For wholemeal flour the whole grain is ground, with its outer layer and germ.
98164.m: Wholemeal means the whole grain is in it.

98165.q: What does wholemeal bread do compared with white bread?
a: It keeps you full for longer
98165.e: The body digests the fibre in wholemeal slowly. That is why you stay full for longer.
98165.m: Wholemeal bread keeps you full for a long time.

98166.q: Where in the grain are there lots of vitamins and minerals?
a: In the outer layer and germ
98166.e: The outer layers and the germ are especially rich in vitamins. In wholemeal bread they are kept.
98166.m: The outer layer and germ are full of vitamins.

98167.q: How can you often recognise wholemeal bread?
a: By bits of husk in the bread
By a hole in the middle
98167.e: In wholemeal bread you often see small dark bits. These are pieces of the grain's outer layer.
98167.m: You can see bits of husk in wholemeal bread.

98168.q: Which bread does the Swiss food pyramid especially recommend?
98168.e: The food pyramid advises choosing wholemeal cereal products. They contain more valuable nutrients.

98169.q: What does yeast do in bread dough?
98169.e: Yeast forms small gas bubbles in the dough. This makes the dough bigger and lighter.

98170.q: What does the yeast produce in the dough that puffs it up?
98170.e: The yeast produces the gas carbon dioxide. It makes lots of small bubbles in the dough.
98170.m: The yeast's gas bubbles make the dough big.

98171.q: Where does a yeast dough rise best?
98171.e: Yeast works best in warmth. In the cold the dough rises only very slowly.

98172.q: What is yeast that you buy as a powder in a sachet called?
98172.e: Dried yeast is yeast that has been dried. It keeps much longer than fresh yeast in a block.
98172.m: Dried yeast is yeast as a powder.

98173.q: What does the yeast in the dough feed on?
98173.e: The yeast eats sugar that comes from the starch in the flour. In doing so it produces gas.

98174.q: Where do the many holes in bread come from?
98174.e: Gas bubbles form while the dough rises. When it bakes, the dough sets and the holes stay.
98174.m: The holes in bread are gas bubbles.

98175.q: What happens to the yeast in the hot oven?
98175.e: The heat in the oven kills the yeast. That is why the bread stops rising after that.
98175.m: Yeast dies in the hot oven.

98176.q: Instead of shop-bought yeast, what can you use to make bread rise?
98176.e: Sourdough is an old, fermenting dough. It makes bread rise and gives it a slightly sour taste.

98177.q: Which four ingredients does a simple bread dough need?
98177.e: For a simple bread, flour, water, salt and yeast are enough. Other ingredients are not needed.
98177.m: Bread needs flour, water, salt and yeast.

98178.q: What do you do with bread dough to make it nice and stretchy?
98178.e: Kneading makes the dough smooth and stretchy. That way it can rise well later.
98178.m: Bread dough must be kneaded well.

98179.q: What does a yeast dough do when it rests covered?
98179.e: During the resting time the yeast works. The dough grows to about twice its size.

98180.q: What do you add when the dough sticks to your hands too much?
a: A little oil in the dough
98180.e: Flour soaks up moisture. That is why the dough sticks less afterwards.
98180.m: A little flour helps against sticky dough.

98181.q: What do you use to roll dough out flat?
98181.e: A rolling pin is a roller made of wood. You use it to roll the dough out thinly.
98181.m: A rolling pin makes dough flat.

98182.q: What do you usually cover dough with while it rises?
98182.e: A cloth keeps the dough warm and stops its surface drying out.
98182.m: A cloth protects the dough while it rises.

98183.q: What is the hard, brown outer layer of a loaf called?
98183.e: During baking, the surface of the dough gets hot and dry. This forms the crispy crust.
98183.m: The crust is on the outside of the bread.

98184.q: What is the soft inside of a loaf called?
98184.e: The crumb is the soft, light part of the bread. You can see the holes from rising in it.
98184.m: Inside the bread is the soft crumb.

98185.q: On which day do people in Switzerland traditionally eat Zopf, a plaited loaf, for breakfast?
98185.e: Zopf is the typical Sunday bread in Switzerland. People like to eat it with butter and jam.
98185.m: Zopf is the Swiss Sunday bread.

98186.q: What goes into Zopf dough but not into a simple bread?
98186.e: Zopf dough is made with milk and butter. That is why Zopf is soft and tastes delicious.

98187.q: What do you brush on the Zopf before baking to make it shiny?
98187.e: Beaten egg is brushed onto the Zopf. In the oven it then turns golden brown and shiny.
98187.m: Brushed with egg, the Zopf shines.

98188.q: How does the Zopf get its shape?
a: It is pressed into a tin
It is rolled into a ball
98188.e: Long strands are formed from the dough. These are plaited together like hair.
98188.m: A Zopf is plaited from strands of dough.

98190.q: Which figure made of sweet yeast dough is baked in Switzerland for St Nicholas Day?
98190.e: The Grittibänz is a little man made of yeast dough, similar to Zopf dough. People eat it around 6 December.
98190.m: On St Nicholas Day there is a Grittibänz.

98191.e: Zopf is a yeast dough. The yeast makes it light and airy.

98192.q: What is the Zopf named after?
98192.e: The loaf looks like plaited hair. In German this hairstyle is also called Zopf.
98192.m: The Zopf looks like plaited hair.

98193.q: Which cereal is spelt closely related to?
98193.e: Spelt is a close relative of wheat. It can be used for baking in a similar way.
98193.m: Spelt is a relative of wheat.

98195.q: What still has to be removed from spelt after threshing?
98195.e: In spelt, the grains stay firmly inside their husks. They have to be removed separately in the mill.
98195.m: Spelt grains sit in tough husks.

98196.q: What is spelt called that is harvested unripe and dried?
98196.e: Green spelt is spelt harvested when half ripe. It is dried and tastes a little smoky.
98196.m: Green spelt is spelt harvested unripe.

98197.q: How long has spelt been grown?
98197.e: Spelt has been grown for thousands of years. It also has a long tradition in Switzerland.

98198.q: What are the tough husks around the spelt grain for?
98198.e: The husks wrap the grain like a protective jacket. They are only removed in the mill.
98198.m: The husks protect the spelt grain.

98199.q: What can you bake with spelt flour?
98199.e: Spelt flour is good for baking. It is used to make bread, Zopf and biscuits.
98199.m: Spelt flour is good for baking.

98200.q: Where does rice very often grow?
98200.e: Many rice fields stand under water. Rice needs a lot of water and warmth.
98200.m: Rice often grows in fields under water.

98201.q: In which canton is the best-known rice field in Switzerland?
98201.e: Rice has been grown near Ascona in Ticino since the 1990s. It is one of the most northerly rice fields in the world.

98202.q: Which dish is cooked with rice?
98202.e: Risotto is a creamy rice dish from Italy that is also popular in Ticino. Polenta is made from maize.

98203.q: What is cooked from rice, milk and sugar?
98203.e: For rice pudding, rice is cooked slowly in milk. With sugar and cinnamon it becomes sweet.
98203.m: Rice pudding is sweet rice in milk.

98204.q: Which group of plants does rice belong to?
98204.e: Rice is a cereal, just like wheat. Its grains grow in a panicle.

98205.q: What is rice called that still has its brown outer layer?
98205.e: Brown rice only has its outermost husk removed. The brown layer stays on.

98206.q: What do people in many Asian countries eat rice with?
98206.e: In China, Japan and Korea people often eat with two chopsticks. You can eat rice well with them too.
98206.m: In East Asia people eat with chopsticks.

98207.q: What do millet grains look like?
98207.e: Millet grains are tiny, round and usually pale yellow. They are much smaller than wheat grains.

98208.q: Where is millet an especially important food today?
98208.e: Millet grows even where it is hot and dry. That is why it is very important in Africa and parts of Asia.
98208.m: Millet grows even in heat and drought.

98209.q: Which cereal can people eat who must not eat gluten?
98209.e: Millet contains no gluten, a protein found in wheat, spelt or barley. Some people get ill from it.

98210.q: What does the magic pot cook in the fairy tale “Sweet Porridge”?
98210.e: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale, a little pot cooks so much millet porridge that the whole town fills up with it.
98210.m: The fairy tale “Sweet Porridge” is about millet porridge.

98211.q: What did many people in Switzerland often eat made from millet in the past?
98211.e: Before the potato arrived, millet porridge was an important food. Millet is easy to cook.
98211.m: In the past, people often ate millet porridge.

98212.q: Which pets like to nibble at millet sprays?
98212.e: Millet sprays are a popular food for pet birds. The birds peck off the small grains.

a: It is roasted in the oven
98213.e: Millet is cooked in water, similar to rice. Afterwards it is soft and fluffy.

98214.q: Apart from millet grains, what else made from millet can you buy?
98214.e: Millet is also rolled into flakes, similar to oats. You can add them to muesli.

98215.e: The oat grains are warmed and then pressed flat between rollers. This makes flakes.
98215.m: Oat flakes are oat grains rolled flat.

98216.q: Which Swiss breakfast is made with oat flakes and apples?
98216.e: For Bircher muesli, oat flakes are mixed with grated apple, milk or yoghurt.
98216.m: Bircher muesli is made with oat flakes.

98217.q: Which Swiss doctor is Bircher muesli named after?
98217.e: The Zurich doctor Maximilian Bircher-Benner made muesli well known around 1900.
98217.m: Bircher muesli comes from the doctor Bircher-Benner.

98218.q: What is a warm dish of oat flakes cooked in milk called?
98218.e: Porridge is an oat dish. It is a popular breakfast, especially in Great Britain.
98218.m: Porridge is warm oat flakes cooked in milk.

98219.q: Which animal traditionally likes to eat oats?
98219.e: Oats are a classic food for horses. They give them a lot of strength.

98220.q: What are oat flakes made from whole grains called?
98220.e: Jumbo flakes are rolled from whole grains. Fine flakes are made from chopped grains.
98220.m: Jumbo flakes are made from whole oat grains.

98221.q: Why are oat flakes considered a wholegrain product?
a: They contain a lot of sugar
98221.e: For oat flakes, the whole grain with its germ and outer layers is rolled. Only the outer husk is removed.
98221.m: Oat flakes contain the whole grain.

98222.q: What happens to oat flakes when you soak them in milk?
98222.e: The flakes soak up the milk and swell. This makes them soft.

98223.q: What can you bake from oat flakes, butter and sugar?
98223.e: Oat flakes are good for crunchy biscuits. They are mixed with butter, sugar and flour.
98223.m: You can bake biscuits from oat flakes.

98224.q: In a tally chart, how many upright lines do you draw before you draw the line across?
98224.e: You draw four lines next to each other. The fifth line is drawn across them.
98224.m: Four lines and one line across make a group of five.

98225.q: How many groups of five do you need in a tally chart for the number 10?
98225.e: Each group stands for 5. Two groups are 5 plus 5, so 10.
98225.m: Ten is two groups of five.

98226.q: A tally chart shows two groups of five and three single lines. How many is that?
98226.e: Two groups are 5 plus 5, so 10. Add 3 lines and that makes 13.
98226.m: First count the groups, then the single lines.

98227.q: Three groups of five and one single line: which number is that?
98227.e: Three groups are 5 plus 5 plus 5, so 15. With the single line it is 16.
98227.m: You can count groups of five quickly in fives.

98228.q: What do you use a tally chart for?
98228.e: You make a line for every thing you spot. That way you don't lose track while counting.
98228.m: With a tally chart you can easily keep count.

98229.q: Lea counts red cars and ends up with four groups of five. How many red cars did she see?
98229.e: Each group stands for 5. Four groups are 5 plus 5 plus 5 plus 5, so 20.
98229.m: Four groups of five make twenty.

98230.q: Why do you always group five lines together in a tally chart?
98230.e: You can count the groups in fives: 5, 10, 15. That is much faster than counting each line on its own.

98231.q: How do you write the number 7 in a tally chart?
a: One group of five and 2 lines
One group of five and 7 lines
98231.e: One group stands for 5. Then add 2 more lines, because 5 plus 2 is 7.
98231.m: Seven is one group of five and two lines.

98232.q: Tim counts 8 blackbirds and 12 sparrows in the garden. How many more sparrows are there?
98232.e: You work out 12 minus 8. That makes 4.
98232.m: You find the difference with a take-away sum.

98233.q: What are the horizontal lines of a table called?
98233.e: Rows go from left to right, like the lines in a book.

98234.q: What are the vertical lines of a table called?
98234.e: Columns go from top to bottom. Each column often has a heading at the top.
98234.m: Columns run from top to bottom in a table.

98235.q: What is usually at the very top of a table, in the first row?
98235.e: The headings say what is in each column. That way you understand the numbers below.
98235.m: Headings explain what is in the table.

98236.q: A table says: apple 7 children, banana 5 children, pear 3 children. How many children is that altogether?
98236.e: You add all the numbers together: 7 plus 5 plus 3 makes 15.
98236.m: For the total, you add all the values together.

98237.q: What do you call a single box in a table?
98237.e: Where a row and a column meet there is a box. It is called a cell.
98237.m: A box in a table is called a cell.

98238.q: Which plan from school is a table?
98238.e: In the timetable the days are in columns and the lessons are in rows. That is a table.

98239.q: A table says: Monday 3 degrees, Tuesday 7 degrees. How many degrees warmer was it on Tuesday?
98239.e: You work out 7 minus 3. On Tuesday it was 4 degrees warmer.
98239.m: A table makes it easy to compare values.

98240.q: What is a table especially handy for?
a: Writing down data in an orderly way
98240.e: In a table every piece of information has its fixed place. That way you can find everything again quickly.
98240.m: A table brings order to data.

98241.q: What does a longer bar in a bar chart mean?
98241.e: The longer the bar, the bigger the number it shows.
98241.m: A long bar stands for a lot.

98242.q: How do the bars in a bar chart usually lie?
98242.e: In a bar chart the bars lie across. If they stand upright, it is called a column chart.
98242.m: Bars lie down, columns stand up.

98243.q: The bar for dogs is 6 squares long, the one for cats is 4 squares. One square stands for one child. How many more children like dogs?
98243.e: You work out 6 minus 4. Two more children like dogs.
98243.m: You find the difference between two bars by taking away.

98244.q: A bar chart shows: red 5, blue 8, green 3. Which colour has the longest bar?
98244.e: 8 is the biggest number. That is why the bar for blue is the longest.
98244.m: The biggest number gets the longest bar.

98245.q: What does the shortest bar in a bar chart show?
98245.e: A short bar means a small number. So the shortest one shows the least.
98245.m: The shortest bar shows the least.

98246.q: One square in the chart stands for 2 children. A bar is 5 squares long. How many children is that?
98246.e: Five squares times 2 children makes 10 children.
98246.m: Always check what one square stands for.

98247.q: Two bars are exactly the same length. What does that mean?
98247.e: Bars of the same length show the same number.
98247.m: Bars of the same length stand for the same amount.

98248.q: What does every bar need so you know what it stands for?
98248.e: Next to each bar there is a word, for example “dog” or “cat”. Otherwise nobody knows what it means.

98249.q: What do the numbers on the axis of a bar chart show?
a: How old the person who drew it is
98249.e: There is a row of numbers along the axis. You use it to read off which number a bar shows.
98249.m: You read off the values on the axis.

98250.q: What do you do in a survey?
a: You ask lots of people the same question
98250.e: In a survey you ask many people the same thing. Then you count up the answers.
98250.m: In a survey you ask lots of people the same thing.

98251.q: In a class of 20 children, 12 answer yes and all the others answer no. How many say no?
98251.e: You work out 20 minus 12. 8 children say no.
98251.m: The yes and no answers together make all the children.

98252.q: Why may each child answer only once in a class survey?
98252.e: If someone answers twice, their opinion counts twice. Then the result is distorted.
98252.m: Each person counts only once in a survey.

98253.q: What is best to decide before a survey?
a: The question and the answers to choose from
98253.e: If everyone gets the same question with the same answers, the results are easy to count.
98253.m: A good survey has a clear question.

98254.q: How do you quickly note down the answers in a survey?
98254.e: For each answer you make a line in the right row. That way you have counted them all at the end.
98254.m: You count survey answers with tally marks.

98255.q: What do you call what comes out at the end of a survey?
98255.e: After counting, you know how many people gave which answer. That is the result.
98255.m: At the end of a survey there is the result.

98256.q: 25 children are asked: 10 like football, 8 like swimming and the rest like cycling. How many like cycling?
98256.e: 10 plus 8 makes 18. Then you work out 25 minus 18, which is 7.
98256.m: You find the rest by taking away.

98257.q: What do you call the people who answer in a survey?
98257.e: Anyone who is asked and answers is one of the respondents.
98257.m: Respondents give answers in a survey.

98258.q: In a vote with two options, how many votes does the majority have?
98258.e: A majority has more than half of all the votes. It wins the vote.
98258.m: A majority is more than half.

98259.q: There are 24 children in a class. What is the smallest number of votes needed for more than half?
98259.e: Half of 24 is 12. So more than half is at least 13.
98259.m: A majority needs one vote more than half.

98260.q: 15 children want to go to the zoo, 10 children to the woods. Where does the trip go if the majority decides?
98260.e: 15 is more than 10. That is why the zoo has the majority.
98260.m: In a vote, the side with more votes wins.

98261.q: What do you call the smaller group in a vote?
98261.e: The group with fewer votes is the minority.
98261.m: The smaller group is the minority.

98262.q: What is it called when both sides have exactly the same number of votes?
98262.e: When the votes are equal, neither side has the majority. This is called a tie.
98262.m: With equal votes nobody has the majority.

98263.q: When is a proposal accepted in a simple vote?
a: When there are more yes votes than no
When there are more no votes than yes
When only one person says yes
98263.e: If there are more yes votes than no votes, the proposal is accepted.
98263.m: More yes than no means accepted.

98264.q: In which two cantons do people still vote by raising their hands at an open-air assembly, the Landsgemeinde?
98264.e: At the Landsgemeinde the voters gather outdoors. The majority of raised hands is counted.
98264.m: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden have a Landsgemeinde.

98265.q: Out of 9 children, 5 vote yes. Do the yes votes have the majority?
98265.e: Half of 9 is four and a half. 5 is more than four and a half, so it is a majority.
98265.m: With 9 votes, 5 is enough for a majority.

98266.q: Rolling a 7 with an ordinary dice: what is that?
98266.e: An ordinary dice only has the numbers 1 to 6. So you can never roll a 7.
98266.m: There is no 7 on an ordinary dice.

98267.q: The sun will rise again tomorrow morning. What is that?
98267.e: The Earth turns once every day. That is why the sun rises every morning, even if clouds hide it.
98267.m: Something that always happens is certain.

98268.q: A little bag holds 9 red balls and 1 blue one. Which colour will you probably pick?
98268.e: There are many more red balls than blue ones. That is why red is much more likely.
98268.m: You are more likely to pick what there is more of.

98269.q: A little bag holds only red balls. What is picking a red ball?
98269.e: There is no other colour in the bag. Every ball you pick is red.
98269.m: If only red is inside, you are certain to pick red.

98270.q: How likely is it to snow in the city of Zurich in July?
98270.e: In July it is usually warm in Zurich. Snow in the city practically never happens then.
98270.m: Something that hardly ever happens is unlikely.

98271.q: You toss a coin. Which is more likely, heads or tails?
98271.e: A coin has two sides. Each side is just as likely to land on top.
98271.m: With a coin, heads and tails are equally likely.

98272.q: A little bag holds 3 green and 3 yellow balls. Which colour are you more likely to pick?
98272.e: There are the same number of balls of each colour. So neither colour is more likely.
98272.m: The same number of balls means the same chance.

98273.e: Impossible means that something cannot happen in any case.
98273.m: Impossible is the opposite of certain.

98274.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: 3 red and 1 blue. Where is it more likely to stop?
98274.e: Three of the four sections are red. That is why the spinner is more likely to stop on red.
98274.m: More sections of one colour means more chances.

98275.q: What do the dots on two opposite sides of a dice add up to?
98275.e: On an ordinary dice, opposite sides always add up to 7. For example, the 3 is opposite the 4.
98275.m: Opposite sides of a dice add up to seven.

98276.q: Which number is opposite the 1 on a dice?
98276.e: Opposite sides add up to 7. 7 minus 1 is 6.
98276.m: The six is opposite the one.

98277.q: How many corners does a dice have?
98277.e: A dice has four corners at the top and four at the bottom. That makes 8 altogether.

98278.q: How many dots does a dice have on all six sides together?
98278.e: You work out 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5 plus 6. That makes 21.
98278.m: All the dots on a dice add up to 21.

98279.q: You roll two dice. What is the biggest total you can roll?
98279.e: The highest number on a dice is 6. Two sixes make 12 together.
98279.m: With two dice you can roll at most twelve.

98280.q: You roll two dice. What is the smallest total possible?
98280.e: The smallest number on a dice is 1. Two ones make 2 together.
98280.m: With two dice you roll at least two.

98281.q: What are the dots on a dice called?
98281.e: The dots on a dice are called pips. For example, you say: “I rolled six pips.”
98281.m: The dots on a dice are called pips.

98282.q: Who is in 1st place on a results list?
98282.e: Whoever did best is in 1st place. He or she has won.

98283.q: In the sprint, Ana runs 9 seconds, Ben 8 seconds and Cem 10 seconds. Who wins?
98283.e: In running, whoever takes the least time wins. Ben only takes 8 seconds.
98283.m: In a race, the shortest time wins.

98284.q: In the long jump, Mia jumps 3 metres, Noah 2 metres 50 and Lina 3 metres 20. Who is in 1st place?
98284.e: In the long jump, the furthest jump wins. 3 metres 20 is the furthest.
98284.m: In the long jump, the longest jump wins.

98285.q: Lia is in 2nd place, Max in 4th. How many children are between them on the results list?
98285.e: Between 2nd and 4th place there is only 3rd place. There is one child there.

98286.q: How many people stand on the podium at a medal ceremony?
98286.e: The top three stand on the podium. The winner stands highest in the middle.
98286.m: The top three stand on the podium.

98287.q: Which medal do you usually get for 2nd place?
98287.e: 1st place gets gold, 2nd place silver and 3rd place bronze.

98288.q: Which medal do you usually get for 3rd place?
98288.e: The bronze medal is for third place.

98289.q: Five children have a race. What place is the slowest child in?
98289.e: With five children there are places 1 to 5. The slowest child comes last, so in 5th place.
98289.m: With five people taking part, 5th place is last.

98290.q: What is the average of 2 and 4?
98290.e: 2 plus 4 makes 6. Divided by 2 numbers, that makes 3.
98290.m: The average is in the middle.

98291.q: What is the average of 3, 5 and 7?
98291.e: 3 plus 5 plus 7 makes 15. 15 divided by 3 makes 5.

98292.q: What is the average of 10 and 20?

98293.q: What is the first thing you do when working out an average?
98293.e: First you add all the numbers together. Only then do you carry on working with this total.
98293.m: For the average, you first add everything together.

98294.q: You have added all the numbers together. What do you divide the total by to get the average?
a: By how many numbers there are
98294.e: You divide by how many numbers there are. With three numbers you divide by 3.
98294.m: You divide the total by the number of values.

98295.q: A team scores 1, 2 and 3 goals in three matches. How many goals is that on average per match?
98295.e: 1 plus 2 plus 3 makes 6 goals. 6 divided by 3 matches makes 2.
98295.m: On average two goals were scored per match.

98296.q: What is the average of 4, 4 and 4?
98296.e: If all the numbers are the same, the average is exactly that number. 12 divided by 3 makes 4.
98296.m: If all the numbers are the same, the average is that same number.

98297.q: In the morning it is 6 degrees, at midday 8 degrees and in the evening 10 degrees. What is the average temperature?
98297.e: 6 plus 8 plus 10 makes 24. 24 divided by 3 makes 8 degrees.
98297.m: You can find the average of temperatures too.

98298.q: In a pictogram, one apple picture stands for 2 apples. How many apples do 4 apple pictures show?
98298.e: Each picture stands for 2 apples. 4 times 2 makes 8.
98298.m: You multiply the pictures by their value.

98299.q: One stick figure in a pictogram stands for 5 children. How many children do 3 stick figures show?
