98842.e: The European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) includes ETCS and the railway radio. It is meant to allow cross-border rail traffic without changing systems.

98843.q: How does dynamic lift arise on a wing?
a: From air flowing around the wing
From the low weight of the wing
From hot air in the wing
98843.e: As air flows around it, it is deflected downwards, and a low pressure forms above the wing. This results in an upward force.
98843.m: Lift arises from the flow around the wing.

98844.q: How does lift change when the speed doubles and everything else stays the same?
98844.e: Lift is proportional to the square of the speed. At double the speed, 2 · 2 = 4.
98844.m: Lift grows with the square of the speed.

98845.q: What lift does a wing with an area of 10 m² and a lift coefficient of 0.5 produce at 50 m/s and an air density of 1.2 kg/m³?
98845.e: The formula is F = 0.5 · density · v² · A · coefficient. So 0.5 · 1.2 · 2500 · 10 · 0.5 gives 7500 N.
98845.m: Lift depends on density, speed, area and coefficient.

98846.q: What is the angle between the wing profile and the oncoming air called?
98846.e: With a larger angle of attack, lift at first increases. If it becomes too large, the airflow separates.
98846.m: The angle of attack strongly affects lift.

98847.q: What happens when the angle of attack of a wing becomes too large?
a: The airflow separates and lift collapses.
98847.e: At too steep an angle of attack the air can no longer follow the upper surface. This flow separation is called a “stall”.
98847.m: Too large an angle of attack leads to a stall.

98848.q: Why does an aeroplane extend flaps on its wings when landing?
a: To produce enough lift at low speed
98848.e: Landing flaps increase the curvature and often the area of the wing. This raises the lift coefficient and the aeroplane can approach more slowly.
98848.m: Landing flaps increase lift in slow flight.

98849.q: What do racing cars use upside-down wings for?
a: To produce downforce and press the car onto the road
To take off at high speed
98849.e: An inverted wing produces a downward force. The tyres then grip better and the car can go through corners faster.
98849.m: Racing cars use wings for downforce.

98850.q: Why do aeroplanes need a longer take-off run at high-altitude airfields such as Samedan?
a: Because the air density is lower
Because the runways are steeper there
Because the fuel is heavier there
98850.e: Less dense air gives less lift at the same speed. The aeroplane therefore has to go faster before it can take off.
98850.m: Thin air requires a higher take-off speed.

98851.q: Which force must lift balance so that an aeroplane keeps its height in cruise?
98851.e: In unaccelerated level flight, lift and weight are equal. Thrust, on the other hand, balances air resistance.

98852.q: What does fly-by-wire mean in aviation?
a: Control commands are transmitted electrically through computers to the control surfaces.
The aeroplane is pulled along on a rope.
The pilot moves the control surfaces directly through steel cables.
The aeroplane flies only by radio remote control.
98852.e: In fly-by-wire, electrical wires and flight control computers replace the mechanical cables and linkages. The computers turn the pilot’s inputs into movements of the control surfaces.
98852.m: In fly-by-wire the pilot flies through computers.

98853.q: Which airliner was the first with fully digital fly-by-wire controls?
98853.e: The Airbus A320 flew for the first time in 1987 and entered scheduled service in 1988. It set the standard for later Airbus models.
98853.m: The Airbus A320 brought digital fly-by-wire into civil aviation.

98854.q: Which control replaces the classic control column in Airbus cockpits with fly-by-wire?
98854.e: The sidestick is a small control stick beside the pilot. It only passes on electrical signals to the computers.
98854.m: Airbus pilots fly with a sidestick.

98855.q: What does the flight envelope protection of a fly-by-wire system do?
a: It prevents dangerous flight conditions such as a stall.
It switches off the engines in turbulence.
It controls only the landing gear.
98855.e: The computers know the limits of the aircraft and, for example, do not allow too large an angle of attack. In this way the system protects against operating errors.
98855.m: Fly-by-wire can protect the aircraft from dangerous flight conditions.

98856.q: Why do fly-by-wire systems have several independent computers?
a: So that a single failure does not lead to loss of control
So that the aeroplane flies faster
So that less electricity is used
So that passengers can watch films
98856.e: This is called redundancy. If one computer fails, others take over its job.

98857.q: Which combat aircraft was the first series-built combat aircraft with fly-by-wire controls?
98857.e: The F-16 was deliberately designed to be unstable in order to be especially agile. Without computer control it would hardly be flyable.
98857.m: The F-16 was the first series combat aircraft with fly-by-wire.

98858.q: Which supersonic airliner already had analogue fly-by-wire controls?
98858.e: Concorde transmitted the control commands to the control surfaces electrically in analogue form. A mechanical control system was kept as a backup.
98858.m: Concorde was an early fly-by-wire pioneer.

98859.q: What is the variant called in which the control signals run through optical fibre cables instead of copper wires?
98859.e: Light signals in optical fibres are insensitive to electromagnetic interference. The cables are also lighter.
98859.m: In fly-by-light the signals run through optical fibres.

98860.q: Where does the aircraft manufacturer Pilatus have its headquarters?
98860.e: Pilatus was founded in 1939 in Stans in the canton of Nidwalden. Test and delivery flights take off from the neighbouring airfield at Buochs.
98860.m: Pilatus builds its aircraft in Stans.

98861.q: In which year was the company Pilatus founded?
98861.e: Pilatus Flugzeugwerke AG was founded on 16 December 1939. It is named after Mount Pilatus near Lucerne.

98862.q: What is the Pilatus PC-6 Porter particularly well known for?
a: Taking off and landing on very short runways
98862.e: The PC-6 is an STOL aircraft (Short Take-Off and Landing). It can land on short, unpaved strips and even on glaciers.
98862.m: The PC-6 Porter is a short take-off aircraft.

98863.q: What is the first jet aircraft from Pilatus called?
98863.e: The prototype of the twin-engine business jet flew for the first time on 11 May 2015. The first one was delivered in 2018.
98863.m: The PC-24 is the first jet from Pilatus.

98864.q: What is special about the business jet PC-24?
a: It can also land on unpaved runways.
98864.e: Pilatus calls the PC-24 the “Super Versatile Jet”. It is designed for short and unpaved runways, which is rare for jets.
98864.m: The PC-24 can take off from grass strips.

98865.q: What type of aircraft is the Pilatus PC-12?
98865.e: The PC-12 came onto the market from 1994 and has a turboprop engine. In May 2023 the 2000th one was delivered.
98865.m: The PC-12 is a single-engine turboprop aircraft.

98866.q: What does the Swiss Air Force use the Pilatus PC-21 for?
a: As a transport aircraft for troops
98866.e: The PC-21 is a training aircraft with a turboprop engine. Trainee jet pilots learn on it before they fly combat aircraft.
98866.m: The PC-21 is a training aircraft.

98867.q: Which family of aircraft do the Pilatus PC-7, PC-9 and PC-21 mainly belong to?
98867.e: Pilatus is one of the world’s most important manufacturers of training aircraft for air forces. More than 600 PC-7s were built.
98867.m: Pilatus is known for its training aircraft.

98868.q: From which company did Pilatus take over about 230 employees and the machine park in Emmen in 2024?
98868.e: The company had been making parts for Pilatus since the 1990s, for example fuselages for the PC-21. With the takeover Pilatus expanded its own production of aircraft structures.
98868.m: In 2024 Pilatus took over staff and machines from RUAG Aerostructures Switzerland.

98869.q: What is the only reaction product formed in a hydrogen fuel cell?
98869.e: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen from the air to form water. In the process electrical energy is released, which drives the electric motor.
98869.m: A hydrogen fuel cell emits only water.

98870.q: Which type of fuel cell is mostly used in passenger cars?
98870.e: The proton exchange membrane fuel cell works at below 100 °C and starts quickly. That is important for vehicles.
98870.m: Cars mostly use PEM fuel cells.

98871.q: At what pressure is hydrogen stored in passenger cars such as the Toyota Mirai?
98871.e: Gaseous hydrogen has a low density. At 700 bar enough of it fits into carbon fibre pressure tanks for several hundred kilometres.
98871.m: Hydrogen is stored in cars at 700 bar.

98872.q: What happens at the anode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
98872.e: At the anode hydrogen is oxidised to protons. The electrons flow through the external circuit to the cathode.
98872.m: At the anode hydrogen is oxidised.

98873.q: What is hydrogen called that is produced by electrolysis using electricity from renewable energy?
98873.e: Grey hydrogen mostly comes from natural gas and causes CO2. Only green hydrogen is largely climate neutral.
98873.m: Green hydrogen is made with renewable electricity.

98874.q: Which Hyundai vehicles have been running on fuel cells in Swiss fleets since 2020?
98874.e: From 2020 Hyundai delivered fuel cell lorries of the Xcient Fuel Cell type to Switzerland. Retailers and logistics firms use them for freight transport.
98874.m: Fuel cell lorries run in Switzerland.

98875.q: Why do most fuel cell cars also have a small battery?
a: To store braking energy and cover power peaks
98875.e: The battery takes up energy when braking (recuperation). When accelerating it supports the fuel cell.
98875.m: The buffer battery stores braking energy.

98876.q: Which researcher is regarded as the inventor of the fuel cell in the 19th century?
98876.e: The Briton William Grove built a “gas battery” from hydrogen and oxygen around 1839. It is regarded as the first fuel cell.
98876.m: William Grove invented the fuel cell.

98877.q: What is a traffic control system on the motorway?
a: A system that controls speed and lanes with changing displays
A speed camera for speeding drivers
98877.e: Sensors record traffic density and weather. From this, suitable speed limits and warnings are shown on variable message signs.
98877.m: Traffic control systems adapt the signals to the traffic.

98878.q: Why does a traffic control system lower the speed limit when traffic is heavy?
a: To even out the traffic flow and delay traffic jams
To measure the noise of lorries
98878.e: At similar speeds there are fewer lane changes and braking manoeuvres. The traffic then stays fluid for longer.

98879.q: What is a traffic jam called that arises without an accident or roadworks, simply from braking reactions in dense traffic?
98879.e: When one vehicle brakes, the one behind brakes a little harder. This wave builds up until traffic stops, with no visible cause.
98879.m: A phantom jam arises for no visible reason.

98880.q: What does hard shoulder running (PUN) on Swiss motorways mean?
a: The hard shoulder is opened as a driving lane at peak times.
The hard shoulder is removed permanently.
Cyclists may ride on the hard shoulder.
The hard shoulder is used as a car park.
98880.e: When traffic is heavy, signals above the carriageway show that the hard shoulder may be used. This raises capacity without new building.
98880.m: With hard shoulder running, the hard shoulder becomes a driving lane.

98881.q: What does ramp metering at motorway entrances control?
a: How many vehicles per minute may enter the motorway
The price of the motorway vignette
98881.e: A traffic light at the entrance lets vehicles onto the motorway in measured amounts. This disturbs the traffic on the main carriageway less.
98881.m: Ramp lights meter the inflow onto the motorway.

98882.q: With which sensors in the road surface do traffic control systems often detect vehicles?
98882.e: A vehicle over the wire loop changes its inductance. This makes it possible to measure the number and speed of vehicles.
98882.m: Induction loops count vehicles in the road.

98883.q: Where is the Swiss Traffic Management Centre of the Federal Roads Office (FEDRO) located?
98883.e: From Emmenbrücke in the canton of Lucerne, traffic on the national roads is monitored and controlled across the country. Diversions are also coordinated there.
98883.m: The Swiss Traffic Management Centre is in Emmenbrücke.

98884.q: What distinguishes a network control system from a route control system?
a: It directs traffic onto alternative routes with variable direction signs.
It affects only a single lane.
It regulates pedestrian crossings in cities.
98884.e: A network control system distributes traffic across the whole road network. In a jam it recommends another route using variable direction signs.

98885.q: Which plug type is the standard in Europe for charging electric cars with alternating current?
98885.e: The Type 2 plug was set as the standard by the EU. It allows single-phase or three-phase charging with alternating current.
98885.m: In Europe you charge with alternating current via Type 2.

98886.q: What is the plug system usual in Europe for fast charging with direct current called?
98886.e: CCS extends the Type 2 plug with two additional direct current contacts. One charging socket therefore fits both ways of charging.
98886.m: CCS is the European fast charging standard.

98887.q: What charging power does a wallbox have that charges on three phases at 16 A each and 230 V?
98887.e: The power is 3 · 230 V · 16 A = 11,040 W. That is about 11 kW.
98887.m: Three phases at 16 A give a charging power of about 11 kW.

98888.q: Why does fast charging become much slower once a battery is above about 80 per cent charge?
a: To protect the battery from overheating and ageing
Because the charging point then saves electricity
Because the car is then heavier
98888.e: An almost full battery can no longer take high currents without being damaged. The battery management therefore lowers the charging power.
98888.m: Above 80 per cent a battery charges more slowly.

98889.q: What does bidirectional charging make possible?
a: The electric car can feed electricity back into the house or the grid.
Two cars can charge at the same time at one charging point.
The car charges in both directions of travel.
98889.e: The car battery then becomes an electricity store, for example for solar power from the roof. This is also called vehicle-to-grid.
98889.m: With bidirectional charging the car gives electricity back.

98890.q: What is the charging standard called for very high power in heavy electric lorries?
98890.e: Electric lorries have very large batteries. The Megawatt Charging System (MCS) is meant to allow charging powers in the megawatt range.
98890.m: Lorries are meant to charge with the Megawatt Charging System.

98891.q: What are fast charging stations with powers of 150 kW and more called?
98891.e: HPC stations reach up to 350 kW or more. A suitable car can then recharge plenty of range in about 20 minutes.
98891.m: HPC charging points charge at very high power.

98892.q: At what kinds of places did FEDRO have fast charging stations set up along the Swiss national roads?
98892.e: The Federal Roads Office put out to tender sites at about 100 rest areas for private operators. This is meant to let electric cars charge reliably even on long journeys.
98892.m: FEDRO promotes fast charging stations at rest areas.

98893.q: How many propellers does a quadcopter have?
98893.e: “Quad” means four. Two propellers each turn clockwise and anticlockwise so that the torques cancel out.

98894.q: How does a quadcopter turn about its vertical axis without tipping over?
a: It changes the speed of the clockwise and anticlockwise propellers by different amounts.
98894.e: If the propellers of one direction turn faster, their counter-torque wins out. The body then turns in the opposite direction.
98894.m: Differences in torque make a drone turn on the spot.

98895.q: What is the maximum height normally allowed for drones in the open category in Switzerland?
98895.e: In 2023 Switzerland adopted the EU drone rules. In the open category a maximum flight height of 120 m applies.
98895.m: Recreational drones may fly at most 120 m high.

98896.q: With which authority must you register as a drone pilot in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA)
98896.e: Registration is free of charge through FOCA’s UAS.gate portal. It is required, among other cases, for drones of 250 g or more or with a camera.

98897.q: What does the abbreviation BVLOS mean in drone flights?
a: Flight beyond the pilot’s line of sight
98897.e: BVLOS stands for “Beyond Visual Line of Sight”. Such flights usually need a special permit.
98897.m: BVLOS flights take place beyond visual range.

98898.q: Which combination of sensors usually keeps a drone stable in the air and in position?
98898.e: Acceleration and rotation rate sensors detect every tilt. Satellite navigation such as GPS supplies the position so that the drone can hover on the spot.
98898.m: Drones stabilise themselves with inertial sensors and GPS.

98899.q: What did Swiss Post use drones for in Lugano from 2017?
a: To transport laboratory samples between hospitals
To deliver parcels to private households
To deliver letters to mountain villages
For advertising flights over the city
98899.e: The drones flew blood and laboratory samples back and forth between hospitals. The samples then reached the laboratory faster than by road.
98899.m: Swiss Post used drones for laboratory samples.

98900.q: How old must you be at the least in Switzerland to fly a drone that must be registered on your own?
98900.e: A minimum age of 12 applies in the open category. Younger children may only fly under the supervision of an authorised person.
98900.m: The minimum age for drone pilots is 12 years.

98901.q: What does the unit TEU stand for in container ships?
98901.e: One TEU corresponds to a standard container 20 feet (about 6.1 m) long. A ship’s cargo capacity is given in TEU.

98902.q: Which container ship was the largest in the world by capacity in 2026?
98902.e: The MSC Irina holds 24,346 TEU and is just under 400 m long. It was delivered in 2023 (as of 2026).
98902.m: The largest container ships hold about 24,000 containers.

98903.q: About how long are the largest container ships?
98903.e: The largest ships are just under 400 m long and about 60 m wide. That is almost four football pitches end to end.
98903.m: The largest container ships are almost 400 m long.

98904.q: In which Swiss city does the shipping company MSC, one of the largest container shipping companies in the world, have its headquarters?
98904.e: The Mediterranean Shipping Company is based in Geneva. In 2022 it overtook Maersk and became the shipping company with the largest container fleet.
98904.m: The world’s largest container shipping company is based in Geneva.

98905.q: Who is regarded as the inventor of modern container transport, who in 1956 sent the “Ideal X” on her voyage with containers?
98905.e: The American haulier Malcolm McLean had a converted tanker sail with 58 containers in 1956. This greatly lowered loading costs.
98905.m: Malcolm McLean invented modern container transport.

98906.q: Which canal was blocked for six days in March 2021 by the container ship “Ever Given”?
98906.e: The Ever Given ran aground in strong wind and ended up sideways. Hundreds of ships queued up, which noticeably disrupted world trade.
98906.m: The Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal in 2021.

98907.q: What does “slow steaming” mean in container shipping?
a: Ships deliberately sail more slowly to save fuel.
Ships are powered by steam engines.
98907.e: Fuel consumption rises steeply with speed. Even a small reduction in speed saves a lot of fuel and CO2.
98907.m: Sailing more slowly saves ships a lot of fuel.

98908.q: Through which Swiss ports do containers reach Switzerland by ship on the Rhine?
a: The Swiss Rhine ports near Basel
98908.e: The Rhine ports in and around Basel are Switzerland’s gateway to the sea. Rhine ships bring containers there from Rotterdam and Antwerp.
98908.m: Switzerland is linked to the sea through the Basel Rhine ports.

98909.q: Which programming language is considered the first object-oriented language?
98909.e: Simula 67 was developed in the 1960s in Norway by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. It introduced classes and objects.
98909.m: Simula from Norway was the first object-oriented language.

98910.q: What is the OOP principle called in which an object's internal data is hidden from direct access from outside?
98910.e: With encapsulation, you only access an object's data through defined methods. This keeps the internal state protected.
98910.m: Encapsulation protects an object's data from direct access.

98911.q: What is the ability called whereby the same method call triggers different behaviour depending on the type of object?
98911.e: Polymorphism means “having many forms”. A call such as draw() can have a different effect for a circle than for a rectangle.
98911.m: Polymorphism lets the same call work differently depending on the object.

98912.q: Which computer scientist coined the term “object-oriented” and helped develop Smalltalk?
98912.e: Alan Kay helped develop Smalltalk at Xerox PARC in the 1970s. He is seen as the originator of the term object-oriented programming.
98912.m: Alan Kay coined the term object-oriented.

98913.q: In OOP, what do you call the functions that belong to an object?
98913.e: Methods describe an object's behaviour. Attributes, on the other hand, store its state.
98913.m: Methods determine what an object can do.

98914.q: In OOP, what do you call the data that stores an object's state?
98914.e: Attributes or fields record an object's properties, such as colour or size. Their values make up the object's state.

a: Same name, redefined in the subclass
The method is called too often
The method has no return value
98915.e: With overloading, there are several methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the right one based on the arguments.
98915.m: Overloaded methods differ in their parameters.

98916.q: Which principle hides unimportant details and shows only what is essential about an object?
98916.e: Abstraction models only the properties that matter for the program. Complex details stay hidden.
98916.m: Abstraction shows only what is essential about an object.

98917.q: What do you call a concrete object created from the blueprint of a class?
98917.e: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class. You can create many instances from one class.
98917.m: An object is an instance of its class.

98918.q: Which special method is called automatically when an object is created?
98918.e: The constructor initialises the new object, for example by setting the starting values. In Java it has the name of the class.
98918.m: The constructor prepares a new object.

98919.q: In Python, which method is a class's initialiser?
98919.e: In Python, __init__ is called automatically after a new object has been created. That is typically where you set the starting values of the attributes.
98919.m: In Python, __init__ initialises a new object.

98920.q: What is true of an abstract class?
a: It must not be inherited from
98920.e: An abstract class serves as a template for subclasses. Only a concrete subclass that implements all the abstract methods can be instantiated.
98920.m: You cannot create an object directly from an abstract class.

98921.q: What is an attribute called that belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances?
98921.e: A class variable, marked static in Java, exists only once per class. All objects see the same value.
98921.m: All objects of a class share a class variable.

98922.q: Which access modifier in Java allows access only within the class itself?
98922.e: With private, an attribute or method is only visible in its own class. This supports encapsulation.
98922.m: Private elements are only visible in their own class.

98923.q: Which design pattern ensures that there is exactly one instance of a class?
98923.e: The singleton pattern prevents further instances, often with a private constructor. It is one of the “Gang of Four” patterns.
98923.m: A singleton has exactly one instance.

98924.q: In Python, what is the usual name of the first parameter of an instance method?
98924.e: In Python, the current object is passed explicitly as the first parameter, called self by convention. In Java and C++, the corresponding reference is called this.
98924.m: In Python, self refers to the current object.

98925.q: With which keyword does a class inherit from another class in Java?
98925.e: In Java you write class Dog extends Animal. For interfaces, on the other hand, you use implements.
98925.m: In Java, you inherit with extends.

98926.q: In Java, which class does every class inherit from, directly or indirectly?
98926.e: java.lang.Object is at the top of the class hierarchy. That is why every object has methods such as toString().
98926.m: In Java, every class descends from Object.

98927.q: Which language allows multiple inheritance of classes?
98927.e: In C++, a class can inherit from several base classes. Java and C# only allow single inheritance for classes, but several interfaces.
98927.m: C++ has multiple inheritance of classes.

98928.q: What is the problem called when a class inherits from the same base class by two routes?
98928.e: If B and C inherit from A and D inherits from B and C, it is unclear which version of A's methods applies. The shape of the hierarchy looks like a diamond.
98928.m: The diamond problem arises with multiple inheritance by two routes.

98929.q: What do you call it when a subclass re-implements an inherited method with the same signature?
98929.e: With overriding, the subclass replaces the behaviour of the superclass. In Java you can mark this with @Override.
98929.m: With overriding, a subclass replaces an inherited method.

98930.q: Which relationship between subclass and superclass does inheritance express?
98930.e: A dog is an animal, so Dog can inherit from Animal. The has-a relationship, on the other hand, describes composition.

98931.q: After which computer scientist is the substitution principle for subclasses named?
98931.e: The Liskov substitution principle requires that objects of a subclass can be used anywhere in place of the superclass. It is the L in SOLID.
98931.m: The Liskov principle requires that subclasses can be substituted.

98932.q: Which Java keyword prevents a class from being inherited from?
98932.e: A class declared final cannot have subclasses. One example is the String class.
98932.m: A final class cannot be inherited from.

98933.q: With which keyword do you call the superclass constructor in Java?
98933.e: In Java, super(...) must be the first statement in the subclass constructor. In C#, the counterpart is called base.
98933.m: In Java, you reach the superclass with super.

98934.q: In version control, what do you call saving a set of changes with a description?
98934.e: A commit records a state of the files together with author, time and message. This makes the history traceable.
98934.m: A commit saves a set of changes permanently.

98935.q: Which of these systems is a centralised version control system?
98935.e: With Subversion (SVN), the history is on a central server. Git, Mercurial and Bazaar are distributed systems in which every copy contains the whole history.
98935.m: Subversion works with a central server.

98936.q: What do you call a parallel line of development in version control?
98936.e: In a branch, you can develop changes independently of the main branch. Later the branches are merged again.
98936.m: A branch is a separate line of development.

98937.q: What arises when two people have changed the same line of a file differently and the changes are merged?
98937.e: The system cannot decide automatically which change applies. A person has to resolve the conflict by hand.
98937.m: Contradictory changes lead to a merge conflict.

98938.q: What do you call a fixed marker for a particular state, for example for version 1.0?
98938.e: A tag points permanently to a particular commit. It is often used for release numbers.
98938.m: A tag marks a particular version.

98939.q: Who developed the version control system Git in 2005?
98939.e: Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, wrote Git for developing the Linux kernel. Today Git is the most widely used version control system.

98940.q: What do you call the storage location where a version control system keeps all files and their history?
98940.e: The repository contains all versions and metadata of a project. In distributed systems, every copy has a complete repository.
98940.m: The repository holds the whole history of a project.

98941.q: What is a big advantage of distributed version control over centralised version control?
98941.e: Because every local copy contains the whole history, you can also commit and look at histories offline. Syncing happens later.
98941.m: Distributed version control lets you work without a server.

98942.e: Linus Torvalds wrote Git for developing the Linux kernel. The reason was that BitKeeper, which had been used until then, was no longer available free of charge.

98943.q: What is a commit in Git?
a: A saved state of the project with a description
A new branch of the project
98943.e: With git commit, you save the staged changes as a new state in the repository. Every commit has a message and a unique ID.
98943.m: A commit records a state of the project.

98944.q: Which command adds changes to the staging area in Git?
98944.e: With git add, changes are staged for the next commit. Only git commit saves them in the repository.
98944.m: With git add, you stage changes for the commit.

98945.q: Which two steps does the command git pull combine?
98945.e: git pull first fetches changes from the remote repository (fetch) and then brings them into the current branch (merge). With an option, rebase can be used instead of merge.
98945.m: git pull fetches changes and merges them.

98946.q: With which hash function does Git identify its objects by default?
98946.e: Every commit has a 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 checksum. Newer Git versions also support SHA-256.
98946.m: Git labels commits with SHA-1 hashes.

98947.q: In which file do you specify which files Git should not track?
98947.e: Patterns in .gitignore, such as *.log, exclude files from version control. Typical examples are build folders or password files.
98947.m: The .gitignore file excludes files from Git.

98948.q: Which Git command puts current changes aside temporarily without committing them?
98948.e: git stash stores the unfinished state on a stack and restores a clean working directory. With git stash pop you get it back.
98948.m: git stash puts changes aside temporarily.

98949.q: Which company bought the GitHub platform in 2018?
98949.e: Microsoft took over GitHub in 2018 for about 7.5 billion US dollars in shares. GitHub is one of the largest platforms for Git repositories.
98949.m: GitHub has belonged to Microsoft since 2018.

98950.q: In Git, what is the pointer to the currently checked-out commit or branch called?
98950.e: HEAD usually refers to the current branch and thus to its latest commit. With a “detached HEAD”, it points directly to a commit.
98950.m: HEAD points to the current state in Git.

98951.q: What do you call tests that check a program only through inputs and outputs, without knowing the code?
98951.e: In a black-box test, you test against the specification. The internal structure of the program is not considered.
98951.m: A black-box test only checks external behaviour.

98952.q: Which test checks whether parts that already worked still work correctly after a change?
98952.e: A regression test repeats existing tests after changes. This shows up unintended side effects.
98952.m: Regression tests find bugs newly caused by changes.

98953.q: Who said, in effect, that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence?
98953.e: With this, the Dutch computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra stressed the limits of testing. To be sure there are no bugs, you need formal proofs.
98953.m: Tests can show bugs but cannot prove there are none.

98954.q: What is the testing method called that specifically checks values at the edges of valid ranges?
98954.e: Mistakes often happen at range boundaries, for example using “less than” instead of “less than or equal to”. That is why you test values right at, below and above the boundary.
98954.m: Boundary value analysis tests the edges of value ranges.

98955.q: Which level of testing checks how several components work together?
98955.e: After the individual modules, you test whether their interfaces fit together. System and acceptance tests follow after that.
98955.m: The integration test checks how components work together.

98956.q: Which test is typically carried out by the customer to formally accept the software?
98956.e: In the acceptance test, the client checks whether the agreed requirements are met. After that, the software counts as accepted.
98956.m: With the acceptance test, the customer accepts the software.

98957.q: What do you call the measure of what share of the source code is executed by tests?
98957.e: Test coverage, also called code coverage, is often given as a percentage. But high coverage does not guarantee that there are no bugs.
98957.m: Test coverage shows how much code is tested.

98958.q: Which method divides inputs into groups that probably behave the same and tests one representative of each?
98958.e: You assume that all values in a class are treated the same. This greatly reduces the number of test cases needed.
98958.m: Equivalence classes save test cases by using typical representatives.

98959.q: What is the usual English name for a module test?
98959.e: A unit test checks the smallest testable unit, such as a single function or method. It usually runs automatically.
98959.m: A module test is usually called a unit test.

98960.q: Which Swiss computer scientist wrote the Java test framework JUnit together with Kent Beck?
98960.e: Erich Gamma and Kent Beck wrote JUnit in the 1990s. Gamma is also one of the four authors of the “Gang of Four” book on design patterns.
98960.m: The Swiss Erich Gamma helped develop JUnit.

98961.q: What do you call a stand-in object that simulates a real dependency in unit tests and checks calls?
98961.e: A mock replaces a database, for example, and checks whether it is called correctly. This keeps the test isolated and fast.
98961.m: A mock object replaces real dependencies in a test.

98962.q: What is the statement called with which a unit test checks an expected value?
98962.e: An assertion such as assertEquals compares the actual value with the expected one. If they do not match, the test fails.
98962.m: With an assertion, a test checks the expected result.

98963.q: What are the three phases of test-driven development?
98963.e: First you write a failing test (red), then the simplest code that makes it pass (green). After that you improve the code.
98963.m: Test-driven development follows the cycle red, green, refactor.

98964.q: What does test coverage (code coverage) indicate?
a: What share of the code is executed by the tests
How many bugs the code contains
How many people have checked the code
98964.e: Coverage of 80 per cent means that the tests run through 80 per cent of the lines of code. That does not make the code free of bugs.
98964.m: High test coverage does not automatically mean bug-free code.

98965.q: Which module of the Python standard library is used for writing unit tests?
98965.e: unittest has been in the standard library since Python 2.1 and is modelled on JUnit. pytest is popular but has to be installed separately.
98965.m: Python comes with the unittest module for unit tests.

98966.q: Which property should a good unit test have?
98966.e: Good unit tests are isolated, fast and repeatable. Their result must not depend on which tests ran before.
98966.m: Good unit tests run independently of each other.

98967.q: In which year was the Agile Manifesto published?
98967.e: In February 2001, 17 software developers met in Snowbird in the US state of Utah. There they drew up the Manifesto for Agile Software Development.
98967.m: The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001.

98968.q: Who wrote the Agile Manifesto in 2001?
98968.e: 17 experienced software developers, including Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, met at a ski resort in Utah in 2001. They were looking for shared values for lighter, more flexible methods of software development.
98968.m: The Agile Manifesto comes from developers working in practice.

98969.q: What does the Agile Manifesto value more highly than comprehensive documentation?
98969.e: One of the four values is: working software over comprehensive documentation. Documentation remains valuable but is less important.
98969.m: Agile teams put working software above documentation.

98970.q: How many principles go with the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
98970.e: The manifesto has twelve principles, such as early and continuous delivery of valuable software. They make the four values more concrete.
98970.m: The Agile Manifesto has four values and twelve principles.

98971.q: Which classic process model with strictly consecutive phases is seen as the counterpart to agile methods?
98971.e: In the waterfall model, analysis, design, implementation and testing follow one after another. Agile methods, by contrast, work in short cycles.
98971.m: The waterfall model works through its phases strictly one after another.

98972.q: Which agile method, shaped by Kent Beck, relies among other things on pair programming?
98972.e: Extreme Programming (XP) stresses practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and short releases. Kent Beck described them at the end of the 1990s.
98972.m: Extreme Programming relies on pair programming.

98973.q: What do you call a short requirement from the user's point of view, such as “As a customer, I want ...”?
98973.e: A user story briefly describes who wants what and why. It is a common format for requirements in agile teams.
98973.m: A user story describes a requirement from the user's point of view.

98974.q: Which agile method shows work on a board and limits the number of tasks in progress at the same time?
98974.e: Kanban originally comes from production at Toyota. In software, it limits the work in progress (WIP limit).
98974.m: Kanban limits the number of tasks at the same time.

98975.q: Which role in Scrum is responsible for the product backlog and for maximising the value of the product?
98975.e: The Product Owner orders and maintains the product backlog. They decide what is implemented next.
98975.m: The Product Owner is responsible for the product backlog.

98976.q: What is the maximum length of a sprint in Scrum?
98976.e: According to the Scrum Guide, a sprint has a fixed length of at most one month. Two weeks is common.
98976.m: A sprint lasts at most one month.

98977.q: According to the Scrum Guide, what is the maximum length of the Daily Scrum?
98977.e: The Daily Scrum is a short daily meeting of the developers with a timebox of 15 minutes. It is used to plan the next 24 hours.
98977.m: The Daily Scrum lasts at most 15 minutes.

98978.q: Which role in Scrum supports the team, removes obstacles and makes sure Scrum is understood?
98978.e: The Scrum Master is a servant leader. They help the team and the organisation to use Scrum effectively.
98978.m: The Scrum Master removes obstacles for the team.

98979.q: What kind of process model is Scrum?
98979.e: Scrum works in short sprints and keeps adapting the planning. It was presented in 1995 by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.
98979.m: Scrum was presented by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.

98980.q: Which sport does the term “scrum” come from?
98980.e: In rugby, a scrum is the tightly packed formation of players. In 1986, Takeuchi and Nonaka compared product development to a rugby team.
98980.m: The term scrum comes from rugby.

98981.q: Which event closes a sprint and is used to improve how the team works together?
98981.e: The retrospective follows the sprint review. The team thinks about what went well and what it wants to improve.
98981.m: In the retrospective, the team improves its way of working.

98982.q: What is the shared agreement called on when a piece of work counts as finished in Scrum?
98982.e: The Definition of Done sets quality criteria for the increment. Only when they are met does a piece of work count as done.
98982.m: The Definition of Done sets out when something is finished.

98983.q: What is the usable result of work created during a sprint in Scrum called?
98983.e: Along with the product backlog and the sprint backlog, the increment is one of the three Scrum artefacts. It must meet the Definition of Done.
98983.m: At the end of a sprint there is a usable increment.

98984.q: What is the Unified Modeling Language (UML) used for?
a: To describe software with standardised diagrams
98984.e: UML is a graphical language for classes, processes and use cases. It is maintained as a standard by the Object Management Group (OMG).
98984.m: UML is maintained by the Object Management Group.

98985.q: How are classes shown in a UML class diagram?
a: As a rectangle with name, attributes and methods
As an ellipse with a stick figure
As a circle with a number
98985.e: The rectangle has three sections: the class name at the top, the attributes in the middle and the methods at the bottom. UML grew out of the methods of Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson.
98985.m: In UML, a class is a rectangle divided into three.

98986.q: Which symbol stands for a private attribute in a UML class diagram?
98986.e: In UML, a plus sign (+) means public, a minus sign (-) private, a hash (#) protected and a tilde (~) package. The symbol comes before the attribute name.
98986.m: In UML, a minus sign marks private elements.

98987.q: How is inheritance shown in a UML class diagram?
a: Arrow with an empty triangular head
98987.e: Generalisation is shown by a solid arrow with a hollow triangle pointing from the subclass to the superclass. Diamonds stand for aggregation and composition.
98987.m: UML shows inheritance with a hollow triangle arrow.

98988.q: Which UML diagram shows the sequence of messages between objects over time?
98988.e: In a sequence diagram, lifelines run vertically and messages run horizontally as arrows. Time runs from top to bottom.
98988.m: A sequence diagram shows the flow of messages over time.

98989.q: What does a line with a filled diamond stand for in UML?
98989.e: In composition, the part cannot exist without the whole. The empty diamond stands for the weaker aggregation.
98989.m: A filled diamond shows composition in UML.

98990.q: Which UML diagram shows actors and the functions a system provides for them?
98990.e: The use case diagram shows actors as stick figures and use cases as ellipses. It describes the system from the user's point of view.
98990.m: A use case diagram shows actors and their use cases.

98991.q: Into which two main groups does UML divide its diagrams?
98991.e: Structure diagrams such as the class diagram show how something is built. Behaviour diagrams such as the sequence diagram show processes. UML 2.5 has seven of each.
98991.m: UML 2.5 defines fourteen types of diagram.

98992.q: What does the abbreviation API stand for?
98992.e: An API is a programming interface through which programs communicate with each other. It sets out which functions are called and how.

98993.q: What is typical of a REST API?
a: Every resource has its own address (URL)
All data is sent in XML envelopes
The server remembers every client permanently
There is only one single function
98993.e: In REST, resources such as /customers/42 can be reached at their own URLs and are handled with HTTP methods. Roy Fielding described the style in 2000.
98993.m: In REST, every resource has its own URL.

98994.q: Which HTTP method does a REST API usually use to read a resource?
98994.e: GET reads data without changing it. POST typically creates, PUT replaces and DELETE deletes resources.
98994.m: You read data from a REST API with GET.

98995.q: Which data format is most often used for exchanging data in modern web APIs?
98995.e: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is easy to read and can be processed by almost all languages. It consists of key-value pairs and lists.
98995.m: Modern web APIs mostly exchange data as JSON.

98996.q: Which older protocol for web APIs packs messages into XML envelopes?
98996.e: SOAP messages consist of an XML envelope with a header and a body. The interface is often described with WSDL.
98996.m: SOAP packs API messages into XML envelopes.

98997.q: What do you call limiting how many requests a client may make to an API in a period of time?
98997.e: Rate limiting protects a service against overload and misuse. When the limit is exceeded, many APIs reply with status code 429.
98997.m: Rate limiting limits the number of API requests.

98998.q: How did the US Supreme Court rule in 2021 in Google v. Oracle on the use of the Java API?
a: As a breach of competition law
98998.e: Google had recreated parts of the Java API for Android. The court ruled that this was permitted as fair use.
98998.m: The US court judged Google's use of the Java API to be fair use.

98999.q: What do you call an API function that still works but is to be removed in future?
98999.e: Functions marked as deprecated should no longer be used in new code. This gives developers time to switch.
98999.m: A deprecated function will be removed in future.

99000.q: Who wrote the GNU General Public License?
99000.e: Richard Stallman wrote the GPL for the GNU project. The first version came out in 1989.
99000.m: Richard Stallman is the author of the GPL.

99001.q: Are you allowed to sell software that is under the GPL?
a: Yes, if the source code is supplied under the GPL
No, it must always be free of charge
Only with permission from the Free Software Foundation
Only if you encrypt the code first
99001.e: With the GPL, free means freedom, not free of charge. You may charge money, but you must give buyers the source code and the same rights.
99001.m: You may sell GPL software, but the freedoms remain.

99002.q: What is the GPL principle called that derived works must be passed on under the same conditions?
99002.e: Copyleft uses copyright to secure freedom. Anyone who changes and distributes GPL software must also release the changes under the GPL.
99002.m: Copyleft requires the same freedoms for derived works.

99003.q: Under which licence is the Linux kernel?
99003.e: Linus Torvalds put Linux under the GPL in 1992. The kernel still uses version 2 of the GPL today.
99003.m: The Linux kernel is under GPL version 2.

99004.q: What does the recursive abbreviation GNU stand for?
99004.e: The GNU project wanted to create a free, Unix-like operating system. The name stresses that it is not Unix.

99005.e: The Free Software Foundation was founded by Richard Stallman in 1985. It is the publisher of the GPL.
99005.m: The Free Software Foundation publishes the GPL.

99006.q: According to the GPL, what must you do if you pass on a GPL program in compiled form?
99006.e: Anyone who distributes GPL software as a binary program must offer the recipients the source code. This keeps the software freely changeable.
99006.m: With GPL software, the source code must be available.

99007.q: Which licence, unlike the GPL, allows changed code to be passed on as closed software too?
99007.e: The MIT licence is permissive and has no copyleft. You only have to keep the licence notice, but you may build the code into your own closed programs.
99007.m: Permissive licences such as MIT do not require copyleft.

99008.q: How many basic freedoms does the Free Software Foundation define for free software?
99008.e: The four freedoms are numbered 0 to 3: to use, to study and change, to pass on, and to pass on improved versions. The GPL protects them.

99009.q: Which flower is often called the “queen of flowers”?
99009.e: The rose has been one of the most popular flowers for a very long time. That is why it is often called the queen of flowers.
99009.m: The rose is known as the queen of flowers.

99010.q: When are garden roses usually cut back hard?
99010.e: In spring, when no more hard frost is coming, old and dead shoots are cut off. Afterwards strong new shoots with flowers grow.
99010.m: Roses are cut back in spring.

99011.q: What colour is the rose given as a sign of love?
99011.e: A red rose has long been a sign of love. People give it on Valentine's Day, for example.
99011.m: The red rose is a sign of love.

99012.q: What are many roses known for when you sniff them?
99012.e: Many roses smell sweet and delicate. Their petals are even used to make scented oil.

99013.q: Which fruit belongs to the same plant family as the rose?
99013.e: The rose and the apple both belong to the rose family. Cherries and strawberries are in it too.
99013.m: The apple is related to the rose.

99014.q: How many petals does a simple wild rose usually have?
99014.e: Wild roses such as the dog rose usually have five petals. Garden roses often have many more.
99014.m: A wild rose usually has five petals.

99015.q: What do you cut off roses in summer so that new flowers come?
99015.e: If you cut off faded flowers, the rose puts its strength into new flowers. That way it flowers for longer.
99015.m: Faded rose flowers are cut off.

99016.q: What does a rose in the garden especially need to flower well?
99016.e: Roses love a sunny spot. In the shade they flower much less.

99017.q: What is a rose that grows up walls and arches called?
99017.e: Climbing roses have long shoots. They are tied to trellises, arches or house walls.
99017.m: A climbing rose grows up walls.

99018.q: What do many people call the pelargonium in the window box?
99018.e: The popular balcony flower is really called a pelargonium. But in everyday life most people say geranium.
99018.m: The balcony geranium is really a pelargonium.

99019.q: What are the wild relatives of the geranium that also grow in Swiss meadows called?
99019.e: Geraniums and cranesbills belong to the same plant family. Their fruits look like a long bird's beak.
99019.m: The cranesbill is a wild relative of the geranium.

99020.q: Which continent do most geraniums come from?
99020.e: Most balcony geraniums originally come from southern Africa. It is warm and sunny there.

99021.q: What can geraniums not cope with at all?
99021.e: Geraniums die in frost. That is why they are brought indoors in autumn.
99021.m: Geraniums must be protected from frost.

99022.q: What do geraniums in pots not like at all?
99022.e: Geraniums need regular watering. But if water is left standing in the pot, their roots rot.
99022.m: Geraniums don't like standing water in the pot.

99023.q: What colour are geraniums in Switzerland very often?
99023.e: There are geraniums in red, pink, white and purple. The best known are the red geraniums.
99023.m: Many geraniums have bright red flowers.

99024.q: What happens with some geraniums when you rub their leaves?
99024.e: With scented geraniums, the leaves smell of lemon or rose, for example, when rubbed. That is why they are called that.
99024.m: Scented geraniums smell when you rub their leaves.

99025.q: Which spot do geraniums like best?
99025.e: Geraniums come from a warm, sunny country. They flower most beautifully in the sun.

99026.q: In which season do sunflowers bloom?
99026.e: Sunflowers bloom in summer, when it is warm and sunny. In autumn the seeds then ripen.

99027.q: What does the stem of a sunflower feel like?
99027.e: The stem and leaves of the sunflower are covered in small, stiff hairs. That is why they feel rough.
99027.m: The sunflower's stem is rough and hairy.

99028.q: In what pattern do the seeds sit in a sunflower?
99028.e: The seeds are arranged in many spirals running to the left and to the right. That way a great many seeds fit on the flower head.
99028.m: The sunflower's seeds sit in spirals.

99029.q: Which insects like to collect nectar from sunflowers?
99029.e: The sunflower's many small flowers offer nectar and pollen. That is why bees and bumblebees like to visit them.

99030.q: Which continent does the sunflower come from?
99030.e: The sunflower first grew in North America. Sailors brought it to Europe a long time ago.
99030.m: The sunflower comes from North America.

99031.q: Which animals like eating sunflower seeds at the bird table in winter?
99031.e: Tits and other birds like pecking at sunflower seeds. The seeds give them a lot of energy.

99032.q: How tall can a sunflower in the garden grow?
a: Only as tall as a shoe
99032.e: Many sunflowers grow two to three metres tall. That makes them taller than adults.
99032.m: Sunflowers can grow taller than a person.

99033.q: What does a sunflower need to grow well?
99033.e: As its name says, the sunflower loves the sun. In a bright, warm spot it grows big and strong.

99034.q: What is the big brown centre of the sunflower really?
99034.e: The centre is made of a great many tiny flowers. Each little flower later becomes a seed.
99034.m: The centre of the sunflower is made of many small flowers.

99035.q: Which country does the dahlia come from?
99035.e: Dahlias grow wild in Mexico. There the dahlia is even the national flower.

99036.q: What do dahlias grow from again each year?
99036.e: Dahlias form thick tubers in the ground. New shoots grow from them in spring.

99037.q: How big can the flowers of some dahlias get?
99037.e: There are very large dahlia varieties. Their flowers can get as wide as a plate.
99037.m: Some dahlias have flowers as big as a plate.

99039.e: Dahlias bloom from summer until the first frost. That way they bring colour to the garden in autumn too.
99039.m: Dahlias bloom from summer into autumn.

99040.q: Which flower colour do dahlias not come in?
99040.e: Dahlias come in almost every colour. But there is no truly blue dahlia.
99040.m: There are no truly blue dahlias.

99041.q: What do pompon dahlias look like?
99041.e: Pompon dahlias have lots of rolled-up petals. That is why their flowers are round like little balls.
99041.m: Pompon dahlias are round like balls.

99042.q: Which animals like to nibble young dahlias in spring?
99042.e: Slugs and snails love the tender young shoots of dahlias. That is why gardeners protect the plants well.
99042.m: Slugs and snails like eating young dahlias.

99044.q: What colours are marigold flowers usually?
99044.e: Marigolds glow a strong yellow and orange. Some also have reddish brown spots.
99044.m: Marigolds have yellow and orange flowers.

99045.q: What do the leaves of marigolds smell like?
99045.e: Marigolds have a strong, spicy smell. Some people like it, others don't.

99046.q: Why do gardeners like to plant marigolds between vegetables?
a: To make the vegetables grow faster
99046.e: The roots of marigolds drive away tiny worms in the soil. This keeps the vegetables healthier.
99046.m: Marigolds protect vegetables from pests in the soil.

99047.q: Which country do many marigolds come from?
99047.e: Marigolds originally come from Mexico and Central America. There they are used to decorate big festivals.

99048.q: How long does a marigold in the garden usually live?
99048.e: Most marigolds are annuals. They are sown again every spring.
99048.m: Marigolds are sown again every year.

99049.q: Which creatures especially like eating marigolds?
99049.e: Slugs and snails love marigolds. That is why marigolds can lure them away from other plants.
99049.m: Slugs and snails love eating marigolds.

99050.q: Until when do marigolds bloom in the garden?
99050.e: Marigolds bloom all summer. Only the first frost in autumn ends their flowering.
99050.m: Marigolds bloom until the first frost.

99051.q: When are pansies often planted on the balcony?
99051.e: Pansies cope well with cold. That is why they bloom in early spring, when other flowers are still asleep.

99052.q: What do the markings on many pansy flowers look like?
99052.e: The dark patches in the middle look like a little face. That is why children especially like this flower.
99052.m: Pansies often have a little face.

99053.q: Roughly how tall do pansies grow?
99053.e: Pansies stay small and grow only about 10 to 20 centimetres tall. That is why they fit well in bowls and boxes.

99054.q: What can you do with pansy flowers in the kitchen?
99054.e: Pansy flowers are edible. You can put them on a salad or a cake, for example.

99055.q: How many petals does a pansy have?
99055.e: A pansy has five petals. The bottom petal is the biggest.

99056.q: Which group of plants does the pansy belong to?
99056.e: The pansy is a kind of violet. Its scientific name begins with Viola, the name of the violets.
99056.m: The pansy belongs to the violets.

99057.e: There are pansies in yellow, blue, purple, white, orange and many mixtures. Often there are several colours on one flower.

99058.q: Where does the wild pansy grow?
99058.e: The wild pansy grows in meadows and fields. Its flowers are smaller than those of the garden kind.
99058.m: The wild pansy grows in meadows.

99059.q: What do hydrangea flowers often look like?
99059.e: Many hydrangeas have big, round flower heads. They are made of many small flowers.
99059.m: Hydrangeas often have round balls of flowers.

99060.q: What does a hydrangea need especially a lot of?
99060.e: Hydrangeas drink a lot. Their scientific name even means something like water vessel.
99060.m: Hydrangeas need a lot of water.

99061.q: What decides whether some hydrangeas flower blue or pink?
99061.e: In acidic soil with aluminium, some hydrangeas flower blue. In chalky soil they turn pink.
99061.m: The soil decides whether some hydrangeas turn blue or pink.

99062.q: Which spot do hydrangeas like best?
99062.e: In blazing sun hydrangeas quickly go limp. They like partial shade best.

99063.q: Which country does the garden hydrangea come from?
99063.e: The popular garden hydrangea comes from Japan. From there it came to Europe.
99063.m: The garden hydrangea comes from Japan.

99064.q: What often happens to hydrangea flowers in autumn?
99064.e: The flower balls dry on the bush and change colour. You can cut them for lovely dried bouquets.
99064.m: Dried hydrangea flowers are good for dried bouquets.

99065.q: Is a hydrangea a tree, a shrub or a grass?
99065.e: Hydrangeas grow as shrubs with several woody shoots. They usually grow about one to two metres tall.

99066.q: What do drooping, limp leaves on a hydrangea usually show?
99066.e: When the soil is too dry, hydrangeas let their leaves and flowers droop. After watering they often recover quickly.

99067.e: Hydrangeas bloom from early summer to late summer. Many flowers last a very long time.

99068.q: What does a lily grow from?
99068.e: Lilies form a bulb made of scales in the ground. A new stem grows from it every year.

99069.q: For which pet are lilies very poisonous?
99069.e: Even a little pollen or a few lily leaves can make cats seriously ill. Cat owners should not have lilies in the home.
99069.m: Lilies are very poisonous for cats.

99070.q: What do many lilies in a bunch of flowers smell like?
99070.e: Many lilies have a very strong, sweet scent. Some people even find it too strong in a room.
99070.m: Many lilies smell strong and sweet.

99071.e: The lily beetle is a bright red beetle. It and its larvae eat holes in lily leaves.
99071.m: The lily beetle is a red beetle that eats lily leaves.

99072.q: How many petals does a lily flower have?
99072.e: A lily has six petals. They often form a trumpet or a star.

99073.q: What colour is the Madonna lily?
99073.e: The Madonna lily has big white flowers. It is a very old garden plant.

99074.q: What can lily pollen do to clothes?
99074.e: Lily pollen is orange brown and stains strongly. That is why it is often picked off cut flowers.

99075.q: Which orange lily grows in sunny meadows in the Alps?
99075.e: The fire lily has bright orange flowers. In the Alps it likes to grow on sunny slopes.
99075.m: The fire lily glows orange in the Alps.

99076.q: Around which festival does the peony often bloom?
99076.e: The peony blooms in May and June. That is roughly the time of Whitsun, which is where its German name, Pfingstrose (Whitsun rose), comes from.

99077.q: In German the peony is called a “Whitsun rose”. Is it a real rose?
99077.e: The peony looks similar but belongs to a plant family of its own. It also has no thorns.
99077.m: The peony is not a real rose.

99078.q: Which small creatures often crawl on peony buds?
99078.e: The buds give off a sweet juice. The ants like it, and they do not harm the plant.

99079.q: What do peony flowers look like?
99079.e: Peonies have big, lush flowers. Many are double and round like a ball.

99080.q: How long can a peony grow in the same spot?
99080.e: A peony can live to a great age. In the same spot it often flowers for decades.
99080.m: Peonies can live for a very long time.

99081.q: What does a peony not like at all?
99081.e: Peonies do not like being moved. After transplanting they often do not flower for several years.
99081.m: It is better not to move peonies.

99082.e: Peonies flower in many shades from white through pink to dark red. There are also yellow varieties.
99082.m: Peonies often flower pink, red or white.

99083.q: What happens to the stems of a garden peony in autumn?
99083.e: In most garden peonies the stems wilt in autumn. In spring the plant grows again from the root.
99083.m: The peony grows again from the root every spring.

99084.q: Which small creatures often sit in crowds on nasturtiums?
99084.e: Black aphids love nasturtiums. That is why they are sometimes planted to lure aphids away from other plants.

99085.e: Nasturtium tastes slightly hot, similar to cress or pepper. This comes from a substance in the plant.

99086.e: The leaves are round and the stalk is attached in the middle. They look like little plates or umbrellas.
99086.m: Nasturtium has round leaves like little plates.

99087.q: What happens to drops of water on a nasturtium leaf?
a: They vanish into the leaf at once
99087.e: The leaves are water-repellent. The drops roll off like pearls and take dirt with them.

99088.q: What colours are nasturtium flowers often?
99088.e: The flowers glow in warm colours such as orange, yellow and red. They attract many insects.
99088.m: Nasturtiums flower orange, yellow or red.

99089.q: Which continent does the nasturtium come from?
99089.e: The nasturtium originally comes from the Andes in South America. Today it grows in many gardens.
99089.m: The nasturtium comes from South America.

99091.q: How does nasturtium often grow in the garden?
99091.e: Nasturtium forms long shoots. It creeps over the ground or climbs up fences.

99092.q: Where can you plant nasturtiums well if you have no garden?
99092.e: Nasturtium needs light and grows well in pots and boxes. The shoots then hang down nicely.
99092.m: Nasturtium grows well in a window box.

99093.q: What does the centre of a coneflower look like?
99093.e: The centre of the flower bulges upwards. That is why it reminds people of a little hat; in German the plant is called “sun hat”.
99093.m: The coneflower has a domed centre like a hat.

99094.q: What colour are the flowers of the purple coneflower?
99094.e: The purple coneflower flowers pink to purplish red. Its centre is orange brown.
99094.m: The purple coneflower flowers pink to purple.

99095.q: What colour is the yellow coneflower?
99095.e: In the yellow coneflower the petals are golden yellow. The centre is almost black.
99095.m: The yellow coneflower has a dark centre.

99096.q: Which continent does the coneflower come from?
99096.e: The coneflower grows wild in meadows in North America. Today it grows in many Swiss gardens.
99096.m: The coneflower comes from North America.

99097.q: Which creatures especially like visiting the coneflower?
99097.e: The coneflower has lots of nectar and pollen. That is why bees, bumblebees and butterflies like flying to it.
99097.m: Bees and butterflies love the coneflower.

99098.q: What is the purple coneflower also used for?
99098.e: Drops and tea are made from the purple coneflower, also called echinacea. They are used for colds, for example.
99098.m: The purple coneflower is a medicinal plant.

99099.q: Does the coneflower come back every year?
99099.e: The coneflower is a perennial. In winter it rests in the ground and sprouts again in spring.
99099.m: The coneflower comes back every year.

99100.q: Which spot does the coneflower like best?
99100.e: The coneflower loves the sun. In a bright spot it flowers abundantly.

99101.q: What colour are forget-me-not flowers usually?
99101.e: Forget-me-nots have small sky-blue flowers. They grow in little clusters.
99101.m: The forget-me-not usually flowers light blue.

99102.q: What colour is the small centre of a forget-me-not flower?
99102.e: In the middle of each blue flower there is a small yellow ring. It shows insects the way to the nectar.
99102.m: The forget-me-not has a yellow centre.

99103.e: The flowers are only a few millimetres across. But there are a great many at once.
99103.m: The forget-me-not has very small flowers.

99104.q: When does the forget-me-not bloom in the garden?
99104.e: The forget-me-not blooms in spring, often together with tulips. After that it fades.

99105.q: How many petals does a forget-me-not flower have?
99105.e: Each small flower has five petals. They are arranged around the yellow centre.

99106.q: What colour are forget-me-not buds often before they turn blue?
99106.e: The buds are often pink. When they open, the flowers turn blue.

99107.q: Where does the water forget-me-not grow?
99107.e: The water forget-me-not loves wet ground. You find it by streams, ponds and in marshes.
99107.m: The water forget-me-not grows by water.

99108.e: The name says: don't forget me. That is why the flower is given as a sign of remembrance.
99108.m: The forget-me-not is a sign of remembrance.

99109.q: What does a robot use to notice what is happening around it?
99109.e: Sensors measure things like light, distance or touch. That way the robot notices what is going on around it.

99110.q: Where do most robots get their energy from?
99110.e: Robots need electricity from a battery or from the socket. Without electricity they don't move.

99111.q: What moves a robot's arms and wheels?
99111.e: Electric motors turn wheels and move joints. Lamps and loudspeakers can't do that.

99112.q: What do you call a robot that looks like a human?
99112.e: Humanoid robots have a head, two arms and often two legs. “Humanoid” means human-like.
99112.m: A humanoid robot looks similar to a human.

99113.q: Who tells a robot what to do?
99113.e: People write programs with commands. The robot carries out these commands.
99113.m: A robot follows a program that people have written.

99114.q: Why are robots often used for dangerous work?
99114.e: Robots can go into very hot or poisonous places, for example. That way people don't have to put themselves in danger.
99114.m: Robots take on dangerous work so that people stay safe.

99115.q: What does a robot lawnmower do?
99115.e: A robot lawnmower drives over the grass by itself and cuts it short. Afterwards it goes back to its charging station.
99115.m: A robot lawnmower cuts the grass all by itself.

99116.q: Which device do you use to type letters into a computer?
99116.e: On the keyboard there is a key for every letter. You use it to write texts.
99116.m: You write on a computer with the keyboard.

99117.q: What do you use to move the pointer on the screen?
99117.e: When you slide the mouse across the desk, the pointer on the screen moves with it. With a click you select something.
99117.m: The mouse controls the pointer on the screen.

99118.q: Which part is known as the “brain” of the computer?
99118.e: The processor calculates and carries out the programs' commands. That is why it is called the brain of the computer.
99118.m: The processor is the brain of the computer.

99119.q: Which two digits does a computer work with deep inside?
99119.e: A computer stores everything as a series of zeros and ones. For it, that means “power off” or “power on”.
99119.m: A computer calculates only with zeros and ones.

99120.q: What is a portable computer that you can flip open called?
99120.e: In a laptop, the screen, keyboard and battery are in one device. You can take it anywhere.
99120.m: A laptop is a computer you can take with you.

99121.q: What do you use to listen to music on a computer without disturbing others?
99121.e: You put headphones directly on or in your ears. That way only you can hear the music.
99121.m: With headphones you can listen quietly on your own.

99122.q: What do you call the texts, pictures and numbers that a computer stores?
99122.e: Everything a computer stores and processes is called data. Photos, songs and texts are data.

99123.q: What do you do when programming?
99123.e: When programming, you write instructions that a computer or robot carries out. Together, these instructions make up a program.
99123.m: When programming, you write commands for computers.

99124.q: What is the well-known programming language for children with colourful building blocks called?
99124.e: In Scratch you drag colourful blocks together and so build a program. You don't have to type in any commands.
99124.m: With Scratch you program using colourful blocks.

99125.q: Which character do you see in Scratch when you start a new project?
99125.e: The orange Scratch cat is the well-known starting character. You can make it move with blocks.
99125.m: The starting character in Scratch is a cat.

99126.q: What does a loop do in a program?
99126.e: A loop carries out the same commands several times in a row. That way you don't have to write them again and again.

99127.q: What do you call a person who writes programs?
99127.e: Programmers write commands for computers. They develop games, apps and much more.

99128.q: At which university did Niklaus Wirth develop the programming language Pascal?
99128.e: Niklaus Wirth was a professor of computer science at ETH Zurich. There, in 1970, he presented the language Pascal, which many people used to learn programming.
99128.m: The programming language Pascal comes from ETH Zurich.

99129.q: What do you call a program on a smartphone or tablet?
99129.e: “App” is short for “application”. An app is a program that you download onto the device.
99129.m: Programs on a smartphone are called apps.

99130.q: What does a robot vacuum cleaner do?
a: It hoovers the floor by itself
99130.e: A robot vacuum cleaner moves around the flat on its own and sucks up dust and crumbs. Nobody has to push it.
99130.m: A robot vacuum cleans the floor by itself.

99131.q: Why does a robot vacuum usually not fall down the stairs?
99131.e: Underneath the robot there are sensors that notice when the floor suddenly ends. Then it stops and turns round.
99131.m: Sensors stop the robot vacuum from falling.

99132.q: Where does the robot vacuum collect the dirt?
99132.e: The dust ends up in a small container inside the robot. You have to empty it regularly.
99132.m: The dirt ends up in the dust container.

99133.q: What shape are most robot vacuums?
99133.e: Because they are flat, they fit under beds and sofas. The round shape helps them turn past furniture.
99133.m: Most robot vacuums are round and flat.

99134.q: What spins on the side of a robot vacuum to get dust out of corners?
99134.e: The little side brush sweeps dust out of corners and from edges. Then the robot can suck it up.
99134.m: The side brush gets dust out of corners.

99135.q: What can an ordinary robot vacuum not do?
99135.e: A robot vacuum only has wheels and is flat. So it can't climb up stairs.
99135.m: A robot vacuum stays on one floor.

99136.q: How does a modern robot vacuum remember where it has already cleaned?
99136.e: Modern robot vacuums measure the rooms and save a map of the flat. That way they know which places are still missing.
99136.m: Modern robot vacuums save a map of the flat.

99137.q: Which part does a voice assistant listen with?
99137.e: The microphone picks up the voice. Then a program works out what was said.
99137.m: A voice assistant listens with a microphone.

99138.q: What does a voice assistant answer with?
99138.e: The voice assistant speaks its answer in a computer voice. You hear it from the loudspeaker.
99138.m: A voice assistant answers through the loudspeaker.

99139.q: What do you usually say first so that a voice assistant listens?
99139.e: Many voice assistants wait for a fixed wake word. Only then do they listen to the request.
99139.m: A wake word wakes up the voice assistant.

99140.q: What does a voice assistant usually need to answer questions?
99140.e: The voice assistant gets many answers from the internet. Without a connection it often can't do much.
99140.m: Most voice assistants need the internet.

99141.q: What can a voice assistant do, for example?
99141.e: Voice assistants can set alarms, play music or tell you the weather. They can't do work with their hands.
99141.m: A voice assistant sets an alarm when you ask it.

99142.q: Which device often has a voice assistant inside?
99142.e: Many smartphones have a voice assistant built in. You can use it to call someone, for example.
99142.m: Many smartphones have a voice assistant.

99143.q: Why shouldn't you tell a voice assistant secrets?
99143.e: What you say is often sent to computers on the internet and can be stored there. So you don't give away private things.
99143.m: Don't tell a voice assistant private things.

99144.e: An AI can get things wrong too and say false things. It sometimes sounds very sure of itself while doing so.

99145.q: What do you call a program you can have a conversation with in text messages?
99145.e: A chatbot answers written questions. Many chatbots work with artificial intelligence.
99145.m: You can write to a chatbot as if it were a person.

99146.q: What can artificial intelligence do, for example?
99146.e: AI programs can translate texts from one language into another. They don't know hunger or tiredness.

99147.q: What should you do when an AI gives an answer?
99147.e: Because an AI can be wrong, you check important answers. For example, in a book or with a teacher.

99148.q: An AI is meant to recognise cats in photos. What does it need first?
99148.e: The AI looks at thousands of cat pictures. That way it learns what cats look like.
99148.m: To recognise things, an AI needs lots of example pictures.
